maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT, 1894.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 149) to amend the Land Titles Act, 1894. He said: This Bill deals with the registration of properties in the North-west Territories, and is intended to remove certain small technical difficulties in the working of the Act. The first clause is to make clear the meaning of section 87. There has already been one amendment but there appears to be a difference of opinion between some members of the legal profession and the judiciary in regard to the effect of the clause. It appears to have the effect as drafted, of preventing the owner himself with dealing with property which he has authorized an attorney to deal with, while the power of attorney is still registered. This will make it clear that the owner can deal with the property as well as the person appointed by power of attorney. Clause 2 is to save the owner of land unnecessary expense in obtaining a certificate of title in lieu of one which has been destroyed. It does away with the necessity of advertising.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton) moved the third reading of Bill (No. 112) to amend the Immigration Act.	[DOT]

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
When the House was in committee on this Bill reference was made to statements emanating 'from the United States immigration service as well as to satements made by the chief officer of that service in the Dominion of Canada. Some very emphatic contradictions were given to the statements which that officer made as to the character of the immigration that is coming into Canada. The United States officer is, apparently, prepared to stand by his statements. It is a matter of vital public interest that our people should know exactly what kind of immigrants are being sent over to this country by the agents employed in Great Britain and on the continent of Europe, or are being brought here by the steamship companies whose vessels reach our ports. I will take the liberty of reading a letter which the United States special immigration inspector, at Montreal, Mr. Watchom, has sent to my kon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson). It is dated, as hon. members will observe, just two days ago :
United States Immigrant Service.
Office of Special Immigrant Inspector.
Port of Montreal, Canada,
233 St. Antoine Street, April 29, 1902.
Uriah Wilson, Esq.,
Member of Parliament,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I desire to thank you for six copies of ' House of Commons Debates,' containing your speech on immigration, delivered on the 17th instant. I note that the editions ar9 still marked 'unrevised,' and I would like to state, that if the revised edition contains any material alterations, I should be very pleased to receive the revised edition ol this debate.
I have noted with considerable surprise, aad not a little amusement, the statements made by the hon. Minister for the Interior, and I venture to suggest that the investigation he male at the hospitals here, was not likely to afford him the information he thought to obtain, because the people diseased as immigrants usually are, are almost invariably enumerated amongst ' outdoor patients,' so chat the mere fact that they were not to he found stretched out On hospital cots, &c., is not a serious answer to the statement that they are here in large numbers, and are afflicted as stated to you, when you were here.
During the month ending to-morrow, the rejections at this office alone, for favus and trachoma, will not fall short of sixty persons. At the very moment I am writing to you, there are more than one hundred Greeks, Syrians, and Italians, at this office, seeking permits to enter the United States. Every one of them was refused passage to the United States, by bona fide lines sailing to United States ports from Europe, and the line that carried them to Canada, refused to soil them tickets, until they Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
had changed their destinations from United States points to points in Canada.
I mention this, in order that you may observe how creditable a thing the hon. minister has done, in introducing the measure alluded to in his speech, contained in the above mentioned debate, and how important a thing it is, that it should be passed as speedily as is consistent with the usages of your honourable parliament.
If I am not asking too much, I would esteem it a favour if you send me a draft of the hill in question, in order that I may observe whether It is calculated to accomplish all that is desirable in this connection.
Thanking you again for the copies of Debates, and for your letter. I am.
Very sincerely yours,
ROBERT WATCHORN, Special Immigrant Inspector.
I think the attention of the minister should be directed to the specific statements that this gentleman makes as to the people who are being brought here by the steamship lines, to whom bonuses are paid by the government, people who, this gentleman says, would positively not be admitted into the United States. Certainly, if these statements are correct, they are not desirable immigrants. This gentleman says :
At the very moment I am writing to you, there are more than 100 Greeks, Syrians and Italians at this office, seeking permits to enter the United States. Every one of them was refused passage to the United States by bona fide lines sailing to United States ports from Europe, and the lines that carried them to Canada refused to sell them tickets until they had changed their destinations from United States points to points in Canada.
The letter is not written, as Is evident, in any unfriendly or hostile spirit. The gentleman who writes the letter approves and endorses the action of the minister in preparing this Bill and he urges its speedy passage. But surely the passage of this BUI is not sufficient. There must be more definite instructions given to the immigration agents of Canada on the continent of Europe and in the old land ; there must be a stricter supervision exercised over tbe immigrants before they go on ship board on the other side of the Atlantic so that this country may not continue to be, as has been asserted again and again, a dumping ground, or a place from which immigrants who could not go from European points direct into the United States may scheme to obtain entrance into that country. That condition of things will no be a benefit to Canada if it is permitted to continue. I direct the attention of the House and of the minister to this letter in order that he may be apprised of the statements which are being made by officers who have been sent here by tbe United States government, who have endeavoured so far as possible to implement the inspection which is made by our own officers, and to prevent undesirable immigrants going into the United States through the Dominion of Canada.

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the place as well as the date of that letter ?

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The heading of the letter is* ' United States Immigration Service, Office of the Special Immigrant Inspector, port of Montreal, Canada, 233 St. Antoine Street, April 29, 1902.' This is addressed to Uriah Wilson, member of parliament, Ottawa, Ontario. I direct the attention of the minister to these statements in order that he may take whatever steps are necessary to put a stop to this class of immigrants being brought here by steamship companies and left in the country until such times as they may be able, if possible, to get through Canada into the United States.

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
When the statements were published that the result of our present system was to leave in Canada a considerable number of persons who started from their place of abode with the intention of going to the United States, and were rejected by the United States inspectors, by reason of disease or otherwise, I did cause an inquiry to be made ; and the result of the inquiry was that out of 25,000 persons who had passed through Canada in a year, there were, of those who had been rejected by the United States commissioner, some 39 people in Canada. Of these 39 people 21 or 23, I am not sure which number, consisted of Germans who had been rejected on account of some trifling complaint in the children of the family. Our medical inspectors, after examining them, permitted them to go to the North-west, being satisfied that these complaints were not of a serious character, and that there was no just reason to compel them to be sent back. That leaves altogether, according to that inquiry, the difference between 39 and 21, or IS persons. That is the result of the inquiry made by the officers of my department. When the statement was made that there was a large number of persons in the hospitals of Montreal who had been rejected by the immigration commissioners, I caused an inquiry to be made there, and I read the result of the inquiry to the House a few days ago, which showed that according to these reports from the superintendents of the hospitals, there was no foundation for the statement that had been made. I should be surprised to learn that when an inquiry of that kind had been officially made of the superintendents of hospitals in the city of Montreal, these gentlemen would deliberately send misleading reports to the Department of the Interior, leaving out a class of patients which they would know if the facts were as stated in this letter, were the very class of patients in regard to whom the inquiry was made. 1 say I should be surprised to learn that gentlemen occupying the position of medical superintendents of these hospitals would have made such misleading reports. It is, I venture to say, improbable, although not
impossible. Now the fact that I have brought this Bill before the House is, I think, sufficient guarantee that the government realize the importance of the subject, and that we propose, as I said before, to take every possible care and precaution for the purpose of carrying into effect the views the hon. gentleman has expressed as being desirable to carry Into effect in the general interest of the country. As to the statement made by Mr. Watchorn, the United States inspector, having heard the statement only now, I cannot say further than this, that recognizing that it is essential that the statement which he has made should be thoroughly, exactly and strictly inquired into, I shall take immediate steps to have that done, and I shall apprise the House of the result in the fullest possible way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would ask the minister, when he is giving us the report as to the accuracy or inaccuracy of these statements, to bring down a copy of the instructions he issued to his officials to make the inquiry from the superintendents of the hospitals in Montreal as to the serious allegations that were made.

maintopic: COMMON'S IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In discussing this subject the other day I made reference to the fact that a good many of these immigrants were affected with dangerous or contagious diseases injurious to the human family. The minister rather denied my statement, and said there were, it is true, a few instances of such people coming in where they might have trifling ailments, but they were comparatively few in number. What I had reference to at the time was a kind of sore eyes, what medical men call granular opthalmia.
I was credibly informed that a large number of them were affected by it. I have in my hand at the present time the ' Canadian Journal of Medicine and Surgery,' printed in Toronto, the number for November, 1901, and I see there an article by Dr. W. Gordon M. Byers, assistant oculist and aurist of the Royal Victoria Hospital, Montreal. Speaking of this ailment, he says :
Two summers ago there came to our clinic at the Royal Victoria Hospital, a young girl from Glengarry county, Ontario, affected with the most intense condition of granular lids 1 have ever seen in Canada. The conjunctures wore covered with heaped masses of succulent granulations, and the cornese showed a condition of highly vascularized pannus.
Then he says later :
A year later, while away on my holidays, I was asked to see a young boy in the county of Leeds, Ontario, for a chronic disease of the eyes. The appearance was at once suggestive, and on everting the lids I found them1 covered wUh tvpical trachoma fol'liciles. Here too, in spite of thie fact that the parents had put themselves to pains, they had been unable to ascertain the real nature of the condition of their boy s eyes, and at no time had they been advised to adopt even the most elementary precautions against tlie spread of the disease.

Since these patients came under my notice I have thought not a -little of the trachoma Dro-biem as it touches our country, and I am persuaded through information and investigation th-at there is a fainiy large number of unrecognized and untreated cases of granular ophthalmia scattered here and there throughout the Dominion. Thus, for instance, I have been informed by m-edtcal friends that t.he disease is comparatively common in certain districts of Manitoba, and even at our hospital the territory from which our trachomatous patients were drawn was extremely broad, our clinics having been visited by patients from' the counties of Glengarry (two centres), Storm-one, Dundas, Leeds (two centres), Renfrew, Lennox, and Car-leton in Ontario ; and Bronte (two centres), St. Hyacinthe, Missis-quoi, Huntingdon and Ottawa in Quebec.
To those acquainted with granular opthailmia, the years of distressing annoyance to he passed by those affected, and the debarm-ent from ordinary work, let alone the higher pursuits and pleasures of life, it must be a matter of apprehension that cases such as I have spoken of should exist unrecognized and unisolated to act as centres of infection throughout the country.
Then he goes on to say :
It stilil remains for me, however, to speak of one strong prophylactic measure. There is- no doubt whatever that the number of our trachomatous patients is being yearly added to by immigrants to this country. Fifteen per cent of the cases of granular opthalmia at the Royal Victoria Hospital Out-Patient Clinic, during the past six years, was of foreign extraction, and among our patients- with this condition- were Russian and German Jews, and a resident each from England, Ireland, China, Italy and Syria. And I scarcely think that the above percentage properly represents the facts, as- the people most likely to suffer from this trouble are settling largely in our western- districts. As an example of what I say, I may mention that I had it on good authority that the cases of sore eyes among the Doukhobors were probably trachomatous in- nature.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 135) to amend the Petition of Right Act (the Minister of Justice), read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

maintopic: PETITION OF RIGHT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Justice to state on what principle the Crown proceeds in withholding or granting fiats for petitions of right. I have had my attention directed to a large number of petitions which were submitted for fiats about two years ago. They relate to contracts between the Crown and persons who carried the mails. The Crown undertook to cancel the contracts under some supposed power contained in the contracts. * Counsel have advised the persons interested that the Crown had no right under the circumstances to cancel those contracts, and that they have good cause for claiming such damages against the Crown as would arise by reason of its having broken the contracts. These matters have been standing about two years. I brought them to the attention of the Postmaster General last evening, but, as the Minister of Justice as well as the Postmaster General is concerned in matters of this kind, I would like to ask him for more information on the subject. I have looked into the cases somewhat hurriedly; but it seemed to me that there was a fair case for the consideration of the courts in respect to a large number of claims, I think thirty or forty-at all events, over twenty; and these people have been held up, so far as any proceedings are concerned, for nearly three years. It appears to me that where there is an arguable case, there should bo no difficulty placed in its way, and I think the House might very well hear from the Minister of Justice at the present time what the policy of the Crown is in regard* to the matter. I have looked into the rule in England, and I do not see anything that would justify the government in keeping these people at bay so long. It seems to me that if there is any tendency at all in this matter, it is to allow the subject the freest possible right to proceed against the Crown. The Postmaster General may think that these claims are groundless, and that he was perfectly justified ini cancelling the contracts; but the real point for the consideration of the House and the country is not what the Postmaster General thinks about it, but what the courts will think about it when these claims are put before them. It amounts to a denial of justice to these people-'because their claims cannot be regarded as frivolous-that they should be held up in this way for a period of nearly three years.

maintopic: PETITION OF RIGHT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: My attention has not been directed, so far as I can recollect, to the cases which the hon. leader of the opposition refers to, and therefore, I would not like to say anything at the present time in reference to them. If they have been before the department for three years, they have probably been disposed of by my predecessor. But the hon. leader of the opposition, I presume, not only wants

maintopic: PETITION OF RIGHT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
to know wliat the reasons may be which necessitated the long delay of the government in granting flats in the cases mentioned, but a statement of the principles which the present Minister of Justice intends to apply in all cases where applications are made for fiats for petitions of right. My hon. friend will understand immediately that that is a question of policy, and therefore, I should not like to state what my personal views are on the subject until such time as I have an opportunity to have those views confirmed by the government. I should not like to say that I would grant a fiat if an arguable case were submitted, if that were my view, because before I state my view, I should like to put it in writing and have the government approve of it, and then place it before the House not merely as my personal view, but the view of the government. I will therefore ask the committee to rise, and when I bring down a statement with reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway matter, I will also make a statement on the point to which my hon. friend has referred; because I quite understand that it is important that the House should have some authoritative statement of the views of the government on that subject.
Mr. CASGIiAIN. I think what the hou. gentleman has just said is perfectly fair and correct. The rule, so far as X have been able to gather it in placing petitions of right before the provincial government and before this government, is this, that when the claim on its face is not frivolous, or when a prima facie claim has been made out, or when there is nothing improper in the claim, the Minister of Justice recommends that a fiat do issue and that a petition be lodged in the court. X think that is the proper rule, which ha^ always been followed in England. My learned and hou. friend the Minister of Justice knows that is the view laid down in Clode on petitious of right. I do not agree with the minister when he says that he does not give his own advice to the House, but would rather submit his views to the government to see whether the views of his colleagues coincide with his own. It seems to me In a matter of this kind that his colleagues should be to a great extent swayed by the Minister of Justice, because after all the thing to be decided is not a question of policy. The question to be decided is not a question of policy. The question is not whether, in the interest of such and such a party, it would be right to grant or refuse the petition, but, whether or not, the petition bears on its face, that stamp of bona fides, which should recommend it to the Minister of Justice as the legal adviser of the government. I have every confidence in the judgment of my hon. friend, and I know that if it were left to him alone, whenever I or anybody else had a bona fide claim before the government, the petition would be granted, but if my hon. friend submits the question to the 124

maintopic: REVISED

speechtext: administration it wll!l Ibe .hard for him to get a unanimous opinion. If this is the rule which is to be followed, in many instances those members of the cabinet who do not belong to tire legal fraternity and cannot see with the same pair of eyes as my hon, friend, would likely set up some other reasons than reasons of law against the granting of the petition. I submit that when he comes down again with this Bill, he should give his own views, as Minister of Justice, as to the course he will follow, and the rule he will carry out when petitions of right are lodged with the government.

maintopic: REVISED
speechtext:
I recollect hearing a very eminent authority in the British House of Commons, say, on a question somewhat analagous to this, that the government could have no opinion except the opinion of the law officers of the Crown. My hon. friend holds a position which corresponds with that of the law officers of the Crown in England, and, as has been well pointed out by my hon. friend behind me (Mr. Cas-grain), this is not so much a question of policy, in the ordinary acceptation of the term, as a question of what is right, from the standpoint of justice, with regard to these petitions. I entirely concur in the view that in respect of matters of this kind the government should adopt the opinion of the Minister of Justice, and, I .should also like to point out that, the provision in this Bill maxing it necessary, when security for costs is ordered, that somebody should give security, goes in the direction of granting the fiat with more liberality than in the past. The only reason why so called frivolous petitions were not allowed in the past was that it was not in the public interest to allow a claim to go to litigation for which there was no foundation and public moneys should not be wasted in .contesting such claims ; but, by the very proper Bill introduced by the Minister o,f Justice, providing that iu certain oases, where it seems expedient to the Governor in Council, security for costs should be given, the fiat should be issued, as a matter of course, on that condition being complied with.
I have no objection, to passing the Bill, as I think it is a proper one, but it is understood we are to have a statement from the Minister of Justice on the subject later in the session.

maintopic: REVISED
speechtext: My view, of course, is that of the government, and my hon. friend has correctly expressed my own view with respect to this question, when he says that this Bill was not introduced merely for the purpose of adding something to the legislation already in existence. The object I have in view is to widen the gate, so far as 1 can, consistent with my duty to the Crown.

maintopic: REVISED
speechtext: When the Bill was first introduced, the argument advanced was that it would assimilate the law in Canada

maintopic: EDITION

speechtext:
to the law in England, where the fiat issues as a matter of right. I understood the Minister of Justice, when introducing this Bill, to say that the fiat would, upon some fixed principle, issue as a matter of right. I think that that is the correct principle. It should not be left to the Governor in Council or the Minister of Justice to say whether a fiat should issue or not, but there should be some fixed rule or principle on which it would issue as a matter of course. In England it is issued almost always as a matter *of course, and when the law was made in Canada the same as that in England, that was done on the understanding that unless there was something very objectionable in the petition for a fiat, the fiat should issue as a matter olf course. I understood from the remarks of the Minister of Justice, when he introduced this Bill, that it was intended to facilitate the granting of fiats. Why should not a man have an action against the Crown just the same as against an individual ? It may be necessary for him to furnish security for costs in the interests of the community, which he might not be requireu to do in a case against an individual, but, upon his so doing, I contend that the fiat should issue as a matter of course, upon a praecipe being filed, just as in the case of an ordinary writ.

speechtext: May I ask why this section only applies to judges of the County Courts ? Does not my hon. friend think that some amendment should be made to the law which would apply also to the judges of the Superior Courts ?

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: If my, lion, friend will look at the law respecting provincial judges he -will find that the judges of the High Court or of the Superior Court, as we in Quebec call it, are entitled, if they become incapacitated after their appointment, to retire at any time upon an allowance equal to two-thirds of the salary, and, at the end \of fifteen years they are entitled absolutely to retire on that allowance, whether they are able to perform their duties or not But the position with respect to County Court judges in Ontario-and elsewhere where they have County Court judges -is such that if a judge lias served less than ten years and becomes unable to perform his duties he is obliged to retire and get absolutely nothing. maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
I was not explicit enough in the question I put. I should have made myself clearer. The purport of my question is really this : My hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) knows that there have been and are still some judges who have rendered good service to the country and who have reached an age when they should be able to retire, not merely with a pension but with an allowance equal to the salary they are now receiving. 1 need not mention names, but my hon. friend, I am sure, knows as well as I do that there are judges of the highest courts of this Dominion and also judges of the Superior Courts of the different provinces who, after serving their country for many years have arrived at an age when it is impossible for them to give the time and assiduity to the fulfilment of their duties which they would wish to give. These gentlemen would willingly retire if it were possible for them to do so. But, because of the smallness of the salary they have received for a number of years-I am not at all in sympathy with those who think salaries of the judges are sufficient- they are not able to retire, but go on in the performance of duties more onerous than those which men in other positions generally undertake at the ages to which they have arrived. I would ask the hon. minister if he does not think that at this stage it would be good policy and further the ad-

ministration of justice to amend the statute so as to provide that when judges have arrived at an age at which men in other professions generally retire, they would be able to retire with a full pension equal to the salary they are now receiving. I am sure my hon. friend is in sympathy with the opinion I have now expressed. I hope that if he is not able at this moment to do what I recommend, in a short time he will be able to see his way to carry out this policy.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: I concur in the remarks which have fallen from the lips of the bon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain). I know that what he says with regard to the position of a number of Superior Court judges is absolutely correct, and what he says applies more to our province than to Ontario, because our Superior Court judges receive only $4,000 a year, while a Superior Court judge in Ontario receives $5,000 from the Dominion and $1,000 a year from the province, a total of $6,000 a year. Now when a judge is in receipt of only $4,000 a year, it is impossible for him to retire under the present provision of the statute. I think the salaries of the judges are too small. Certainly, in the province of Nova Scotia they are much too small. The duties of judges in Nova Scotia are the same and che amount of work is the same as that coming before judges in Ontario. These judges have the disposal of matters of life, liberty and property, and I do not think their salaries should be as low as they are. A judge may become incapacitated, yet he is not in a position to take advantage of the Act as it stands because of the shortness of his term of service. I hope the government will take into consideration this proposed change and will place the judges in a position of absolute independence so that they may know that after they have served a certain time, if they are compelled to retire, they will have a proper retiring allowance, and I think that amount should be equal to their salary.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentlemen who have preceded me are ia the happy position of being private members and so are free to speak their minds. If I were a private member I would like to say that I am in favour, and always have been in favour, of giving proper consideration to the judges of the land. I think the salaries ought to be increased :	I think
also that when a judge has served his country for a period of years-say twenty or twenty-five years-and if he has reached an advanced age as some of our judges have, he should be allowed to retire on full pay. I would have absolutely no sympathy with those who think that our judges now [DOT]are paid, beyond the value of the services they render. I think the judiciary of this country are entitled to every possible consideration at our hands, and we ought to promote in every way 124J
their interests, and especially to provide for their declining years. I know that it is a maxim of the Bar that we live well and die poor. That is a principle with us. Probably there are a good many in this House who are not in sympathy with what I have said ; but as I said a moment ago, when speaking as a private member, one can speak more freely his own mind.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is the second member of the government who has said what he would do if he were a private member. It might be interesting to consider what would happen if all the members of the government were private members. Apparently some very notable reforms would take place in the affairs of this country if that happy consummation could some day be achieved. There is a great deal in what has been said-I am speaking entirely as a private member in this regard-there is a great deal in what has been said in regard to the salaries of the judges. They are very inadequate, because they were fixed years ago at a time when the cost of living was very much less than it is now. In addition to that general increased cost of living, there is a necessity for the judge to keep up a certain appearance, he has to do entertaining, and all these things make the cost of living for a judge very great. I know the judges in our own province have found the salary which is provided for them very inadequate indeed. I should be glad to know that this matter will engage the attention of my hon. friend.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
Not being a lawyer.
1 do not understand this question perhaps as well as the hon. gentlemen who have been speaking. But there is one thing to which I wish to draw the attention of the Hon. Minister of Justice, and which I think is very pertinent in discussing this question. I would like to ask him-I know he has not been very long in his position- if he has any trouble to find gentlemen in the profession who are willing to take a position of judge when it is offered to them ? I have every respect for the judges, but I do not understand why, if they are such a long-suffering community, there are so many in the legal profession who are willing to take a judgeship and to go through all the sufferings and to perform the onerous duties which that position entails upon them-and even to live on starvation allowance. Now, I want to see the judges properly paid, but I do not believe in holding out inducements to them or encouraging them to live extravagantly, to live beyond their means, and then, after a few years, to retire them on an allowance sufficient to keep them in extravagance all their days. I am satisfied in my own mind that there are a great many gentlemen on the bench who receive a great deal more money than they could earn in the practice of their profession.

Although they should be enabled to live respectably and all that sort of thing, there should be no encouragement held out to a judge or any other person to live-extravagantly. They should be taught to use economy and save up money for their declining years, the same as I have to do,' as well as the people of this country generally.

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman was acquainted with the extravagant administration of the Depart-

speechtext: ment of .Justice previous to 1S96, he would not make that remark.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Do I understand that this is a reintroduction of the superannuation System and its application to the judges?

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: It provides that the judges of county courts who have not served ten years on the bench and who become physically incapable of performing their duties may receive a pension.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: It is optional ?

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: No, if they become physically incapacitated they may receive a pension; otherwise, if this Bill is not passed, and they have not served ten years, they will not receive anything.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Why not apply this principle to men in other situations in the public service who get much smaller salaries, and who have less opportunity to put by anything from their meagre incomes ? Why not provide that men getting $600, $800. $1,000, $1,200, and who are compelled to retire on account of physical disability before having served ten years, should likewise receive some consideration ? Surely if judges who receive $4,000. $5,000, $6,000 a year should be looked after, and I think they should, it is equally incumbent on the government, on the same principle of justice, to look after those in receipt of much smaller salaries who spend their lives in the public service, or who have to retire incapacitated before they have served ten or twelve years. If this superannuation system is to be applied to judges, and I think it should, I submit respectfully that it ought to apply to other departments of the public service.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: I do not want it understood that I am opposing the Bill from any remarks I have made. I think the principle is sound.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Although I represent a rural constituency, I am not at all afraid to advocate an increase of salary for the judges. I live in the city of Montreal, where I practice, and I may say that out of twenty or twenty-five bank cashiers, all but two or three receive greater salaries than our judges. The judges in the city of Montreal receive $5,000 a year, and I know at least ten or twelve cashiers, some of them in small banks, who get from $10,000 to $15,000 a year.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: A cashier has to work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
I think a judge is as much entitled to a good salary as a bank cashier. I have known a chief justice, I will not mention his name, who to my knowledge refused to accept invitations because his salary would not enable him to

reciprocate. That is the position in which some of our judges are in Montreal.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot allow some of the remarks that have been made to pass without a protest on my part.
I am not speaking because I think I will ever be a judge. The time seems to be pretty far off if I were ever likely to be called to such an exalted honour. I am speaking because I think that some information should be given to the House on this question at this time. This is a question which has been brought up several times. It was brought up by me two years ago and again last year, and it seemed then to be the sense and the opinion of this House that the judges of this country were not paid high enough salaries. I do not mean to say that is always the case in respect to judges living in rural towns, for instance, as in the province of Quebec, who get the same salaries as the judges living in cities. In the city of Montreal the judges receive $5,000 a year. I would ask any kon. gentleman who knows anything about the cost of living in Montreal if it is possible for a man to occupy the position of a judge and maintain his position on such a salary. He has naturally, from the position which he occupies to reciprocate many kindnesses, to appear in society, to live up to the position he occupies, and I would ask hon. gentlemen if it is possible for him to do so on a salary of $5,000 a year ? Being a citizen of Montreal, living in that city, I venture to say that it is absolutely impossible for a judge to live upon that salary if he wants, as we say in French, to do honour to the position which he occupies. When these salaries were fixed a few years ago the cost of living was not anything like it is to-day. The cost of living has increased by at least 30 per cent since these salaries were fixed by statute 15 or 20 years ago. At that time it was not thought that the salaries were too high; it was thought that the judges were simply getting what they were entitled to. Let me call the attention of the committee to the fact that judges, unlike the managers of large railways companies, or of banks, as my hon. friend for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) said a moment ago, are not only dealing with the fortunes of the people but they are also dealing with the life and liberty of the subject in this country. The duties which they are called upon to fulfil are the most difficult, the most onerous and the most responsible duties that any man could fulfil, and this has been recognized all over the world. I will not mention the salaries paid to judges in England, which run from $25,000 to $35,000 and $45,000 a year, but take the salaries paid to judges in the British colonies, in Australia, in New Zealand and in the Cape of Good Hope, I venture to say there is not one colony where the judges are paid such low salaries as they
are paid in Canada. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that it is becoming a danger to the public at large to have the salaries of judges fixed at the amount at which they are fixed to-day. I shall not call the attention of the committee to any particular incident, but let me just suppose this case for example; let me suppose the case of a man who, from misfortune, or for some other reason, is in debt. Suppose he is a judge upon the bench, suppose he has a case before him, which happens every dav in the city of Montreal, involving $50,000 or $100,000 or $200,000 or $500,000; then, you see the danger there is that this man, being a poor man, being in debt, should be called upon to deal with such large interests. It is not only in the interest of the judges themselves, but it is in the interest of the public as well that proper salaries should be paid. It is not because I think I will curry any favour with them that I am constantly advocating an increase in their salaries, but it is because I think it is in the interest of the administration of justice in this country, and in the interest of litigants that the paltry sum which the judges are receiving should be increased, and that decent salaries should be paid them.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
I think that in the province of Ontario the complaint is not that the Superior Court judges are paid too much, but rather that there are too many judges in the country tumbling one over the other. When hon. gentlemen now on the government side of the House were in opposition, there was one plea they always put forward and that was the plea of economy, and if there was any one question on which the government of that day were attacked it was the question of judges and their salaries. The records of this House will show that when these hon. gentlemen were on the left of the Speaker they assailed from time to time the appointment of county court judges as being unnecessary and superfluous in the province of Ontario. What does the record show ? Here we find, in the province of Ontario, that there are 45 senior county court judges and 23 junior county court judges, making in all G8 county court judges in that province. I say it is simply a burlesque and travesty that in the province of Ontario there are county court judges who are simply sitting around and waiting for something to do. We remember the abuse that was heaped upon the Conservative administration in times past, but, hon. gentlemen opposite have gone on doing the thing which they condemned. Take, for instance, the county of Ontario. In the county of Ontario a little time ago there was a vacancy in the junior judgeship. The government, in obedience to the demands of party friends, appointed a junior judge in that county. What do the records show there ? I will not state from memory

the exact number of cases that were dealt with in that county, but I am bound to say that there were less than six cases tried in the county of Ontario in one year by the two judges.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: What are the salaries which they receive ?

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: I suppose they get the regular salaries-the senior judge, $2,600, and the junior judge, $2,000. The country is not paying enough salary to the Superior Court judges of the province of Ontario. I will not make any invidious distinctions. There are some gentlemen who occupy places on the Superior Court bench of Ontario, the value of whose services is placed at $7,000, while it is a well known fact that these gentlemen, if they were active in their profession, would earn from $15,000 to $20,000 a year. At the same time, let me tell the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) that there are gentlemen not only in the county courts, but on the Superior Court bench as well, who, I fear would fall very far short of the salaries which they are receiving if they were standing shoulder to shoulder in the ranks and practicing their profession. Therefore, in Ontario, I think any lawyer who is not afraid to speak out his mind, and I am speaking out my mind, knowing that election protests are far ahead-of course saying that in a jocular way-will agree with me that we should endeavour to have fewer Superior Court judges and that we should increase the salary of these judges to $10,000 a year. Then, you will bring the best men in the profession to the bench. Take Mr. Ayles-worth, of Toronto, for instance; he is a gentleman who would not look at a position worth $7,000 a year. I assume that Mr. Aylesworth makes three times that, and probably mox-e. This business of the county court judges is simply a farce. They are falling over one another in the province of Ontario, and yet they are paid the salaries which I have mentioned. I know one gentleman who is receiving annually $2,600 as county court judge. In addition he will have the fees commuted to him from the Surrogate Court, the fees from arbitrations, revision of the voter's lists and other matters. That gentleman's salary will run up to $3,500 a year, and I will be bound to say that in days past, when he was practicing at the bar, he never saw $1,500 a year, and would not have seen it had he continued to practice at the bar. Some means should be taken by the government, in so far as county court judges are concerned, to see that there shall be fewer county court judges and fewer Superior Court judges, particularly in the province of Ontario. I do not speak for any other province because I know nothing about other provinces, but in Ontario let us have fewer county court judges, let us have fewer Superior Court judges, and let the

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Superior Court judges be paid salaries that will be commensurate with the abilities! they so fittingly bring to the positions which they occupy. The Minister of Justice could have told the House that had one of the judges of the other courts gone to the Court of Appeal, he would have forfeited $1,000 a year. These judges, who are only human like other men, weigh up the dollars and cents, and so prefer to stay where they are. Once again, let me place myself upon record as a lawyer in saying : We should have fewer judges in the province of Ontario, and the Superior Court judges should be paid a higher salary. Start at the root of the matter, and that is the county court judgeship business.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Inasmuch as I entirely dissent from almost all my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) has said, I think it my duty to say a word or two on this question. I do agree that the Superior Court judges of Ontario are not paid as they should be paid, and I believe their salaries should be greatly increased. I do not agree with the hon. gentleman '(Mr. Bfennett) that the number of Superior Court judges in that province should be decreased. I believe that if there was a lesser number of judges they could not discharge their duties properly. They now work harder than most men do at the bar ; they get behind their work, and it would be impossible for fewer judges to do the work. To talk of reducing the number is entirely out of the question. The salaries paid to our judges are so meagre that I agree with the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) that it is dangerous to the public at large to allow the remuneration of judges to remain at so low a figure. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say that if some of the judges were practicing at the bar they would not earn a sum equal to their present salaries, but it is a fact that we have on the bench of this country, men who did not become eminent as members of the bar, but when in some cases make better judges than those who before their elevation to the bench had a very large practice.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
If a judge occupies the position with dignity and gives perhaps better satisfaction as a judge than his brother judge who was eminent at the bar, surely that man is entitled to receive at least equal compensation to him who was the more eminent practitioner if he discharges his judicial functions equally well. Comparisons between men on the bench and men at the bar are not always a fair test of the standing on the bench. This is true as regards the judiciary in all British countries. The smallness of the salaries paid to our judges is a grievance recognized by the members of the Bar throughout Canada, and the sooner it is

remedied the better for the country. In England, eminent members of the legal profession are able to go on the bench without making such a pecuniary sacrifice, because the salaries paid are so large that a man can maintain his rank and dignity in the eyes of the public. I agree with the statement that certain members of the Bar in Ontario are earning three times the salary which is paid to a judge. That is an anomaly which should not be allowed to exist in any country. I trust that the government, and especially the Minister of Justice, will take this matter in hand, and that before long Canadian judges will receive such a salary as will enabe them to maintain the dignity of their position. What the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) said regarding our county court judges is to some extent correct. There are some county court judges who have pretty nearly nothing to do, but there are others who are overworked. To adjust this state of affairs is a task of considerable difficulty, because we are bound by county boundaries. we are bound by appointments which were made years ago and which have been repeated, and the present occupants of the office have certain vested rights which I do not suppose that even my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) would argue should be interfered with. Might I throw out the suggestion, that the junior judge could be taken from a county where there is not much work, and when a vacancy occurs in a county where there is a great deal of work transferred there, and no new appointment made in the county which he left. In this way no injury would be done to the individual and there would be a saving to the country.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: (Translation.) The hon. member from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) and my hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) have assumed the role of prophets, but they are by no means the only ones who have taken that position, as several other gentlemen who belong, I think, to the legal profession, have spoken to the same effect. I do not wish to impute any motives to the hon. gentlemen and to insinuate that some of them are expectant judges

There is a very important consideration that was lost sight of by those who are in favour of increasing the salaries of judges, and it is that they are paid a retiring allowance when they retire from the bench. However, I agree that the salaries of judges are below the emoluments derived by leading members in the practice of the legal profession ; but those lawyers are an exception to the rule, and besides, the question of income should not be the sole test of efficiency or fitness for a seat on the bench. So long as the leading members in the practice of their profession, and so long as even members of this House, as is often the case, will be ready to give up their positions in order to accept judgeships, there is no reason to take alarm if their salaries are not increased.
Some lion, gentlemen have contrasted the salaries of judges and the salaries given to bank cashiers ; but there is no comparison at all between those positions. I admit that we have bank officers, bank presidents and bank cashiers, and others who are paid much higher salaries than even the highest salary that is paid to judges of the land. But one must not jump to the conclusion that, because higher salaries are given in commercial life and monetary institutions, the salaries of judges must be increased.
So long as leading men at the bar, who are most renowned for their accomplishments and their integrity, men who are successful in the practice of their profession, and who, therefore, are fit to disenarge the duties of the judiciary will be ready to accept judgeships ; so long, I say, as there will be such a keen competition as is now the case, among those who wish to rise to the bench, and who are all well qualified for the position, I think there is no reason of taking alarm and to fear disasters for the country and for those who are amenable to the tribunals of justice, if the salaries of judges are not increased.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved that the House again go into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: ['Friday, May 2, 1902.']

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to bring to the attention of the House a matter, the importance of which I deem will warrant its consideration for a short time. I had intended originally to bring it in the form of a motion, and, had I done so, I should have asked the hon. mem ber for Toronto West (Mr. Clarke) to second the motion. I presume, however, that it will answer just as good a purpose to discuss the question without putting into your hands a motion in relation to it. The question I desire to bring to the attention to the House is in regard to the advisability on the part of the government of rendering aid to a Canadian expedition for the purpose of discovering or seeking to discover the north pole.
The question may perhaps be raised as to the advisability of making the expenditure which would be necessary for this purpose. I shall endeavour to show that such an appropriation would serve the public interest and would be worth to the country more than the sum of money required. We are, of course, making large expenditures; the country is bearing a considerable burden; but, in a growing and young country like Canada, it is necessary to make appropriations which perhaps the future will derive the benefit from, and will be called upon to liquidate ; and the question is whether the expenditure which I shall urge on the government on this occasion is an expenditure of that character or not. We have recently awakened to the possibility of having an active and aggressive national life in Canada. We no longer feel like apologizing for being Canadians. We no longer have that sense of provincialism, possibly I might say of inferiority. that was once entertained bv citizens of this country. We have found,'in bringing back the sheaves of achievement from South Africa, which have cost us some blood and tears, that we have gained an enviable position in the world, a position which has drawn the attention of the world to Canada, a position which is worth infiu-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
itely more in the results which it will bring in the present and the future than all tlie sacrifice in money and life that has been given to purchase it. Now, Sir, it is probable that the expenditure which I shall urge upon the government on this occasion is one which will bring to Canada a large meed of reputation throughout the world, and will give to ourselves the idea that we are progressive, that we have capabilities, that we may aspire to toe a nation. The proposition to send a Canadian expedition to the north pole is not a visionary one. The discovery of the north pole in our case would not be a fruitless one. Aside entirely from the reputation that would accrue to this country from the settlement of a geographical problem which has engaged the attention of maritime nations for generations, we would establish our right to all the territories and islands and seas that might lie between our present northern boundary and the north pole itself-all that vast region between the 141st parallel of longitude on the west, and Baffin's Bay and Grant land on the east. And these possessions may be of value. They may contain enormous mineral wealth. Our impression as to the worthlessness of these arctic lands is perhaps an erroneous impression. The temperature of all this great region to the north of latitude 75 is not much, if any lower than that of Dawson.
This prize has been sought for by many notable and daring men-by Scorestoy in 180G. by Parry in 1827, by Sir George Nares in 1870, by De Long in 1879, by Greeley in 1882, by Nansen in 1895, and by the Duke d'Abruzzi in 1899-1900; and there are at this moment two polar expeditions in progress- that of Peary, who will attempt to reach the pole from Greenland, by means of sledge journeys over the ice, and that of Baldwin, who, following the theories of Captain Bernier. of Canada, will attempt to reach it by Franz Joseph Land. It may be that these two American expeditions will forestall us in the discovery of the pole; but even if they did, the credit that would accrue to us from an expedition would be quite sufficient to compensate us for its cost.
I think .it may be asserted without any question that Canada is peculiarly well fitted for this work. We have hardy and daring seamen in our maritime provinces; we are constantly exploring the wilds; we have exploring expeditions in progress every year-Tyrrell in the North-west, Low in Labrador, Bell and others to the north-east and east of James Bay, and other Canadian explorers; and the accomplishments of these men warrant me in saying that we have an aptitude for this kind of work-hardihood. courage and aggressiveness-that specially fits us for undertaking it. The whole history of Canada back to the time the first French colonists landed in this country is a history of adventure and daring. While the English colonists explored the country

only as far west as the Alleghany Mountains, the French colonists penetrated Into the far Interior, to the valley of the Mississippi, and up tihe Ottawa river to the great lakes. La Salla explored the great west almost to the mouth of the Mississippi. Duquesne Hounded a posit on the site of the great industrial centre of Pittsburgh and Alleghany city, near which subsequently a British army under Braddock was overwhelmed and annihilated. These explorers established posts at Detroit, Mackinaw. St. Louis, and other points in the west. These daring hardy men led the van in the march of the empire and were perfectly well a ware of the grea t value of the possessions they had secured toy their explorations, but the supine, effete dynasty in power at Versailles had not the courage, the grasp or tihe prescience to avail themselves of these explorations, and so Canada fell into the hands of Britain, and we are today in the position to utilize in the same race these admirable qualities which marked the early explorers of the North-west.
We want. I imagine, to add to the exploits of the past. We want to do something to keep up the prestige of the past, and we can do this, in my opinion, with as little expense, and as easily by reaching the North Pole in advance of all other maritime nations as in any other way. The accumulations of knowledge and experience with regard to Arctic voyages and conditions will place whoever commands a Canadian polar expedition to-day in a position far more favourable than that in which any previous navigator has been placed.
We have various theories with regard to the Arctic basin. We have the old and exploded theory of an open Polar Sea and various other theories. We have discovered various facts which have an important bearing on explorations, and one of the most important is the ice drift first discovered by Gustave Lambert in 1866. Careful investigations have shown that there is a regular movement of ice from that portion of the Arctic Sea. situated next to Behering Straits, and extending across to the east coast of Greenland, so that a vessel, packed in that ice will drift across the Arctic Ocean. It was in consequence of that theory that DeLomg placed the ' Jeannette ' in the ice drift, and later on wreckage from the vessel was found thousands of miles away on the coast of Greenland. In persuit of this theory the ' Fram,' under command of Captain Nansen, entered in the ice near the north-east coast of Siberia nearly north of the mouth of the Lena river and drifted on to within 285 miles of the pole. This knowledge of the ice drift was taken advantage of by DeLong and Nansen, and we now have experience and knowledge more full and complete and more likely to lead to a successfid result than has ever been possessed by any Arctic navigator at any previous time. This experiment of Nansen's enabled him to reach latitude
86T3, within 227 miles of the pole. Following him, the Duke d'Abbrezzi approached the pole 20 miles nearer, or within 207 miles. This theory of the ice drift simply amounts to this, that an explorer, by his knowledge of the direction of the currents. can place his vessel in filie drift and trust himself to nature and nature's God to drift towards his destination. There has been a theory propounded regarding the possibility of reaching the pole by means of vessels similar to the one now used in the Baltic, which are able to crush ice of the thickness of II feet. This is. however, probably an impracticable method. Thg information I have sought to place before the House with regard to the knowledge now in the possession of those who have given attention to the matter, will warrant our coming to the conclusion that it is worthy of our consideration at least as to whether we shall avail ourselves of the services of some one thoroughly competent to pursue and profit by the investigations, and invest a little money in the hope of placing Canada at the head of all maritime powers in the search for the North Pole.
I wish now to state that we have among Canadian navigators a nautical man, whose experience, whose courage, whose length of service in seafaring life, and whose knowledge of all the conditions pertaining to Arctic exploration, probably render him better fitted than any other man in this country, and as well fitted as any in the world, to take command of an expedition and attempt to reach the North Pole. I refer to Captain Bernier, who belongs to the race of La Salle, which has penetrated to the heart of the continent, and who has the courage to undertake to penetrate to the North Pole, and will do it if the government will afford him the means. Captain Bernier is 50 years old. If the government had done their duty and sent him at the time they should have, he would have started on his trip at 48 years of age. He was in command of a vessel at the age of 17. He has commanded 46 ships. He has crossed the Atlantic 174 times. He has never lost a vessel except in one instance, when he ran the ' Quorm ' ashore to save her from going to the bottom, she having sprung a leak, and the investigation of the underwriters exonerated him from all blame, as also did the owners of the vessel. He was for twenty years with IV. H. Ross & Company as captain, overlooker, and repairer, filling these various capacities in the service, in all quarters of the world. He was eight years with P. Baldwin, ship builder at Quebec. In the summer he took the vessels across to their destination, which were constructed, and in the winter lie acted as superintendent of the ship yard and superintended the construction of twelve ships. He was with the Richielieu Company two years, and adjusted the compasses on all their vessels, eleven in number. He sailed on the government steamer 'Eureka' with the

Minister of Public Works, on a tour around the gulf and the coast, and no doubt the hon. minister will give a good testimonial as to his capacity and qualifications.
His theory of reaching the North Pole, which is to place his vessel in the ice north of Behring Straits and drift to its destination, has been endorsed by Lord Minto and Lord Strathcona, and I consider the endorsa-tion of Lord Strathcona as one of particular significance, because Lord Strathcona spent many years of his life in the far north and is thoroughly conversant with the conditions of the Arctic regions-probably better fitted than any man who represents Canada to give an intelligent opinion as to the probability of Captain Bernier succeeding in the expedition he proposes to take. The Captain's theory has been endorsed by the Colonial Institute. His theory was accepted and endorsed by the Institute and Sir Clemens Markham, on January 16th, 1901. It was endorsed also by the Royal Society, by resolution of 23rd May, 1901. The Canadian Institute of Toronto endorsed it in 1901, and it also received the eudorsation of the Ontario Surveyors Association. Captain Bernier has addressed members of this House in Room 16 on two occasions-once in the year 1900. at a meeting of which the Minister of Finance was chairman. I believe that Capt. Bernier then succeeded in convincing every one who listened to him of the feasibility of his plan for reaching the North Pole. He again addressed the members of this House on March 23rd, 1901, at a meeting of which my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Edwards) was chairman, and again enlisted the sympathy and commanded the confidence of the great majority of those who listened to him. He has a certificate of competency from the American Consul Henry at Quebec, and he has a great number of testimonials that universally and emphatically assert that he is a sea-faring man possessing the qualifications, the capabilities and the knowledge that peculiarly fit him for the position he seeks with regard to this matter. He has I believe, the endorsation of one hundred and thirteen members of this House, who have signed a petition to the government asking that the necessary appropriation shall be made to enable him to carry into effect the plans that he has promulgated and laid before us.
Now', with regard to the plans for this expedition, I thiuk it is as well to enter into these in some detail. Captain Bernier proposes to build a vessel of wood. A vessel of wood is much better adapted to the purposes of Arctic navigation and navigation among ice floes than is a vessel of steel. The vessel will be built upon the west coast as it will enter upon its service by passing through Behring Straits. It will be of the same plan as the ' Fram,' which was commanded by Nansen, but ten tons heavier-being three hundred tons net measurement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
She will be of the same general plan as the ' Gauss,' now being constructed at Kiel, for the German expedition to the south pole. It will be built with the utmost strength in order to resist the ' ice mips ' as they are called-that is, when a vessel is caught between fields of ice which either crush her like an egg shell or lift her out of water. The vessel will have a system of wa ten tight compartments, six in number, which, no previous Arctic vessel has had, and which will add enormously to her strength and power of resistance. She will be 120 feet keel, 35 feet beam, and IS feet deep, and will have a flush deck, which is a new and desirable feature, in the opinion of the captain. The vessel will have a draught of 14 feet; she will have three masts and will be top sail schooner rigged. She will have triple expansion engines, a 10-foot wheel, two boilers, each 10 feet of diameter and 8 feet long, and will be of 200 horse power, and able to steam at full steaming capacity on three tons of hard coal for every twenty-four hours. She will have a spare rudder and a spare wheel and will be fitted with a diving apparatus, which, no other Arctic vessel has had. The captain himself is a practical diver, and can examine his vessel if she has received an injury or spring a leak, and can ship a new rudder or put in a new wheel. The vessel will carry 300 tons of anthracite-not bituminous-coal. It is found that bituminous coal will not do for Arctic navigation; the cold converts it into slack, and so its steaming qualities are greatly reduced. Anthracite will remain intact and perfectly good for steaming purposes for the period he would require to use steam. She will have-and here is a new feature-two wind-mills for the purpose of pumping the vessel and running the dynamos, and she will have electric light and electric heating apparatus. The old fashion w-as to illuminate the vessel by means of lamps. One lamp would consume in an hour as much air as a person would consume in three hours. The result was that Arctic vessels were invariably dark, damp and uncomfortable. The plan of Captain Bernier would light the vessel without the consumption of air, and enable him to keep the vessel dry, getting rid of this feature of dampness and securing cheer and comfort in place of the conditions that have hitherto existed in Arctic vessels in the six months darkness of a polar winter. This feature alone, as compared with the old condition of things, might give an advantage that would just measure the distance between success and failure. The vessel will carry a complete Dr. Dawsing's electrical apparatus, including an X-ray apparatus which will be most useful in cases of rheumatism swelling and other ailments. The expedition will carry-and this perhaps, is the strongest feature that could be named as tending to ensure success-a wireless telegraph apparatus. The captain will communicate with Dawson regularly, and,
3957	MAY 1, 1902	3958
if conditions, are favourable, lie will be able to communicate with Hamervest in Norway. He will also be able to communicate with sledge parties that leave the ship, and would be constantly in communication with the base of supplies and headquarters. These sledge parties equipped with wireless telegraph apparatus would have an enormous advantage as compared with the conditions that existed under the old system. Under the old conditions, when a sledge party was sent out, the ship might be moved with the field of ice in which she was imprisoned, or the parties might lose their course owing to the storms, and, when they returned, perhaps might not find the ship in the position in which they left it, and might search for it for days before they found it. With the wireless telegraph apparatus, these parties will know the position of the ship at any moment, and the vessel will know where the sledge parties are, and can be kept informed as to their operations and their needs. The vessel will carry a water distilling and filtering apparatus. Hitherto vessels engaged in Arctic exploration have depended for their water upon melted snow, which is often impregnated with salt. Often the crews are compelled to use water with a solution of five per cent of salt. But with an apparatus I have mentioned there will be a means of distilling and filtering the water, which is a matter of the utmost importance-it is a guarantee against scurvy and various kinds of sickness, Captain Bernier will take 100 tons of provisions, sufficient for six years. There will be fresh vegetables and fresh meat in fifty pound cans or boxes, square in shape to facilitate packing; kiln dried flour, kiln dried oatmeal, beans biscuits containing 10 per cent of albumen, coffee, tea, cocoa-an abundance of healthful, wholesome provisions of all kinds. With such an outfit of provisions, that scourge of Arctic expeditions, scurvy will be entirely avoided.
Captain Bernier's crew will be so organized as to combine efficiency and economy. The crew will consist of fifteen men. There will be the commander himself, without pay. There will be two officers, captains of experience, who can take the wheel, go to the mast-head and look-out, or perform any duty regarding the navigation or care of the ship in case of the captain being incapacitated. There will be a first mate who will be what is termed an ice master, a man who is thoroughly conversant with everything pertaining to the dangers of ice and of being caught between ice floes. There will be two engineers; one will be a machinist who can do any work in connection with the machinery or apparatus, the telegraph apparatus or fixtures ; while the other will be an electrician and wireless telegraph operator. Two men will be surveyors and astronomers who will also serve on sledge journeys or in almost any other capacity on the vessel. There will
be one doctor who will be a botanist and seaman. There will be one naturalist, who will be a botanist, photographer and artist and assistant to the surveyors and electrician, and who also will go on sledge journeys. There will be one cook, who, in addition to being a cook and steward will be an able seaman. There will be one seaman who will be a whaler and sealer and stoker, and who will combine the qualifications of all three and be able to serve in almost any capacity. There will be a carpenter who will be also an able seaman, and one stoker who will also be an able seaman. These will be his crew of 15, men combining the qualifications and different kinds of capacities that, if confined in each case to one man, would require a crew of 50 or 60 men, an efficient crew, and yet a compact crew of small number. In addition to these 15 men, the vessel will carry 30 sledge dogs.	.
Now, the government can fit out this expedition with all the instruments that are necessary by merely lending them to it, and they can be returned when the vessel completes its voyage. Captain Bernier will obtain letters from the Russian government to the Siberian officials and to the tribes on the Siberian coast. Had the DeLong party been armed with letters of that kind none of the members of the expedition would probably have been lost. As it was they landed upon an inhospitable coast, they had no credentials to present to the Russian officials, and all the crew were lost except two or three men, who could not obtain assistance to get back to those they had left to rescue them until it was too late. Letters such as the captain proposes to obtain will command the services of the officials wherever he can find them, and will command the services of the native tribes upon the coast as well.
The captain proposes-there is a map upon the Table which hon. gentlemen can examine-the captain proposes to enter Behring Straits and to sail nearly due north until he reaches the ice pack, and he will enter the ice pack between longitude 170 and 175 west, as the openings may dictate to be the proper thing to do. When he enters this ice pack-at a point where his experience and investigations tell him he will probably be able to drift to within 100 or 150 miles of the pole-when he enters this ice pack his vessel will simply be committed to nature to carry it on its course. While in the ice pack drifting towards the pole, and past the pole towards the eastern coast of Greenland. Captain Bernier proposes to send out sledge parties on each side of the vessel for 50 miles and to survey a strip 100 miles in width, to take soundings, and obtain all the information it is possible to obtain by these investigations. When arriving at the point where he is nearest to the pole, he will then organize sledge parties for approach to the

pole; and lie will rely, as lie lias relied before in these lateral investigations perhaps 50 miles each way-he will rely upon dogs, and upon a new feature never before introduced in Arctic sledge explorations, that is, an automobile motor run by a petroleum engine weighing 100 pounds, the sledge weighing 100 pounds; and where the ice is favourable, he will make progress with this motor at three times, perhaps, the rate of speed that dogs would enable him to do. He will have the frames of boats with a canvas covering to launch when he reaches the openings in the ice. Nansen made the mistake, in his expedition, of leaving his boats covered and the covering exposed to the weather, and to the hard usage which rendered the boats useless. Captain Bernier will have the coverings of these boats carefully folded and ready for use, and the frames ready to be covered any moment when he reaches a place where a boat is needed. He will take fur clothing for all the members of the party. The mistake made by Nansen, and' to which the failure to reach the pole was largely due, was that they discarded fur clothing and attempted to make the journey with warm woollen clothing, which they found entirely unsuited for the purpose. Captain Bernier will be enabled to profit by all the mistakes that Nansen made, and enabled to profit by all the experience that Nansen acquired, and will enter upon that race for the pole under circumstances much more favourable than any explorer has enjoyed before.
He will have in this sledge journey regular communication by wireless telegraphy with his vessel. Every half mile, or mile, a hole will be bored in the ice and a hollow tube inserted which will serve as a landmark, and when it is necessary to return there is a line of landmarks one mile apart, and every one of them a storehouse of supplies. Ho has the advantage of availing himself of an instrument which is being perfected, an instrument which I believe has not yet received a name, an instrument which may be termed the guide for the wandering and the lost, an instrument that can be adjusted with another instrument that is adjusted with it. Two parties separated from each other, carrying each of them one of these instruments, though they may be lost in a blinding snow storm, with their points of compass lost, and themselves lost hopelessly, can yet travel towards each other by the use of these instruments ; or they can be gauged with an instrument on board the vessel ; and this little monitor carried by a member of the sledge party, will direct him with as unerring accuracy to the vessel as a needle will direct to the pole. Now, this itself is a matter of great importance indeed. and with all these up-to-date appliances. with all the resources of modern science up to the very day that he starts, at his comamnd, I believe, Mr. Speaker,
