speechtext:
that Captain Bernier, in his race for the pole, has the conditions all in his favour.
What will be the expense ? The captain has secured contributions to the extent of $20,000. He cannot tell, perhaps no one can exactly, what he will require, but the probability is that the government would require to supplement that subscription by a sum of at least $100,000. Now, it may be said: Why should this money be appropriated ? Here are two polar expeditions under way now; perhaps one of these will get to the pole first, and Captain Bernier will be cut out. Well, sir, even if another expedition did reach the pole before Captain Bernier got there, if he succeeded in reaching the pole on the first attempt made, if the first Canadian polar expedition was successful, the credit that would be due to Captain Bernier, the credit that would come to the country from that achievement, would be vastly more valuable than the amount of money required to fit out that expedition. But suppose he got there first, and I believe that will be the case. I do not believe that Peary will get to the pole by a journey from Greenland over the ice ; I doubt whether Baldwin will get to the pole from Franz Josef land. Captain Bernier will go to the place where the currents will set him towards his destination, he will plant his vessel in the ice where the currents, the existence of which he knows perfectly well, will carry him to the place lie wants to reach and then bring him out. He has been investigating this matter for 25 years. His knowledge with regard to this matter has been availed of by Nansen, by Baldwin, and by other explorers, and it is time now, Mr. Speaker, that Canada should have the credit of an achievement that will result largely from the investigations and the knowledge possessed by one or our own sons. If he gets there first, this country will be glad, you will be glad, Mr. Speaker, I will be glad, the premier will be glad, every citizen of Canada will be proud over this achievement of Captain Bernier.
It would have the effect, Mr. Speaker, of a first-class advertisement, one of the finest that could be obtained. It would bring us probably into better odoiir in Great Britain, it would make us better known there. I suppose at this moment that one half of her population would be just as ready to believe that Canadians wear snow shoes all the year, except during an occasional thaw in July and August, and live on blubber and bear meat, as they are to believe that we have 500,000 spuare miles of the finest wheat land in the world, ready to occupy, that we raise the finest grapes, the finest peaches and the finest apples in the world, and have room for 100,000,000 people to be supported from the products of our own soil. We want to -draw their attention to this country, we want to draw their attention a little more fixedly to this Dominion. We would like the

United States people to have their attention directed to this country with a more sincere desire to obtain an intelligent knowledge as to the conditions that exist to-day, as to the physical features of the country and various other things and by means of expeditions and expenditures of this kind that we might enter into we would certainly bring Canada into prominent notice more readily and at less expense than in any other way. We would like to have the attention of the world in general and the world at large, not that we are self conceited, not that we desire to indulge in any vain boasting, but we want the attention of the world in order that Canada may be understood and .iustly appreciated. We want the attention of the world directed to this country which is now swelling with aspirations of national life, which is now deciding upon the course which will lay the foundations of a national future and which must win that position and win it by earning it. We have, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the outset, asserted ourselves. We have taught the world something and we have done something more important than that; we have taught ourselves something. We have taught ourselves what our resources are, what our capabilities are, and this polar expedition would be a nationalizing factor in our experience. It would be an expedition undertaken and joined in by both races and it would be an advertisement to the world and more than this it would be an incentive to aspiration, to great achievements, to high resolves, to self-reliance and to development in national character that would be worth infinitely more than it will cost. I urge, Mr. Speaker, upon the government the advisability of giving the money to place this expedition on foot, to draw the attention of the world to the fact that Canada has sent a polar expedition with the good hope that in due time Canada's effort will be crowned by success and that Capt. Bernier will reach the pole.

speechtext:
I desirp to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) on the very elaborate and convincing presentation of the case which he made this afternoon on behalf of Captain Bernier. I join most cordially with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) in urging the claims of that hardy mariner upon the government. Twelve months ago, when the estimates of the Marine Department were under consideration, I took the liberty to draw the attention of the government to Captain Bernier's project, and I then urged that it was worthy of tbeir serious consideration.
I expressed the hope that the government would be able to see its way to make some appropriation to aid Captain Bernier in the construction of a vessel and the furnishing of its equipment for the expedition to the North Pole. Since then I have had no reason to change my mind. I have been more convinced than ever after listening to the speech of the hon. member for North Norfolk. I believe that the great bulk of the people of Canada .would most cordially sustain the action of the government if it decided to make a substantial grant, say $100,000, to aid Captain Bernier in what I conceive to be little short of a national enterprise. Captain Bernier it seems to me has special claims upon us and upon the government. He has acted most unselfishly in this matter; he has given years of his time, and he has spent considerable of his money in elaborating every detail of the expedition which he proposes to take charge of. He has prepared plans and has submitted them to the most eminent scientific authorities; he has had consultations with the most prominent Arctic explorers, and so correct has he been in his calculations that I think I am right in saying that they have received the approbation and endorsation of the foremost scientific and geological societies of the world. Captain Bernier comes from a family of mariners; his ancestors before him were mariners; he is a mariner himself. Since he was 17 years of age he has had command of ships; he thoroughly understands his business; he is actuated by the highest of motives, and if it is possible fori any man to succeed in this arduous undertaking, that man is Captain Bernier. Ha has patriotism; he has capacity; he has, knowledge; he has intense zeal. These are qualifications which make for success. As( the hon. member for North Norfolk pointed out: If the first Canadian expedition to the Arctic regions should prove successful; if the men who compose that expedition should! succeed in reaching the goal that has been vainly striven for by many daring adventurers in the past; great honour will be reflected upon Canada. From the time the expedition leaves our shores intense interest will be taken in Its progress and its welfare by tlie people of Canada as well as by those of the civilized world. And if it should turn out that Captain Bernier-taking the precautions he has taken; providing for every possible contingency-should succeed in the accomplishment of his great mission, Canada will be placed in a higher position in the estimation of the world than Canada now occupies. Speaking as the representative of an Ontario constituency; speaking as one of the representatives of the city' of Toronto, I believe I am reflecting the public opinion of the great majority of that city when I say:	That they would desire
most cordially to co-operate with the government in giving the necessary aid to Captain Bernier to enable him to equip his

expedition. Every Canadian worthy of the name would rejoice if in the course of two or three years Captain Bernier should return to us safe and sound having accomplished his great object. I cordially support the proposition of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), and I hope that it will receive the most favourable consideration of the right hon. the Prime Minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: It is impossible not to be deeply interested in Captain Bernier, because of his personality, and because of the political considerations connected with his mission as well. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) has said, Captain Bernier has remarkable qualifications for undertaking an expedition of the kind spoken of by the hon. member for North Norfolk. The subject of polar exploration has been so long before the people of Canada and of the civilized world, that such a mission as this requires very little commendation from the lay members of society. Polar exploration in the past has been largely confined to men of scientific attainments, and with strictly scientific objects in view. Should Captain Bernier succeed in obtaining the endorsement of the government and parliament of Canada, he will probably be the first Arctic explorer whose reputation has been established chiefly as a navigator. Hitherto the scientist has taken advantage of the knowledge and skill of the navigator, and the scientist penetrated as far as possible in the Northern Polar seas. But the expedition of Captain Bernier will be in charge primarily of a navigator, and any one who has studied this! most interesting subject cannot but think, that under the guidance of a great navigator and a thorough sailor, as Captain Bernier is, aided by scientific men, there is a chance of accomplishing something that has not been accomplished in the past. It is certain that Captain Bernier has the advantage of the experience of the past, and from the addresses which he has delivered as well as the criticisms which have been made upon his plan, it can easily be seen that he contemplates a thoroughly careful attempt-not to discover the North Pole, as some people imagine the object of the expedition to be- but a thoroughly careful attempt to circumnavigate the polar sea, and to report the conditions in these regions and what they indicate as to the nature of the scientific deductions that may be made from them. It will be recollected by hon. gentlemen who have read Captain Bernier's brochure, that he contemplates a different course from any taken in the past. His idea is to enter the polar sea at the Behring Straits, and taking advantage of the drift and passing as near as possible to the pole, when reaching the point nearest the pole, he expects to make expeditions, aided by the most scientific assistance, to endeavour to reach the pole, and

Mr. Speaker, I cannot add much on this subject to what has been said by the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, further than to concur most heartily in what they have said, and to urge upon the government a compliance with the demand of Captain Bernier to provide him with a sufficient sum to carry out the object he has in view. It may be said, that from the successful carrying out of his project nothing of intrinsic value to Canada will accrue. But from the patriotic standpoint there is certainty this to be said, that it has been the aim of many of the important nations of the world to achieve this object. Every effort has thus far failed, but from the failure of previous efforts a great deal has been learnt, and my firm conviction if that it is possible to succeed in this project, Captain Bernier is the man to do it. Some may say that it would have been more desirable if some highly scientific man were engaged in the project. Well, Mr. Speaker, from my knowledge of the man, if for the carrying out of this project you offered me all the scientists of the world on the one hand, and offered me Captain Bernier as against them, I would take Captain Bernier. So far as the necessary accomplishment is concerned, the characteristics of the Canadian voyageur are the most necesssary elements for the success of such an undertaking. If scientific research is necessary Captain Bernier can have scientific men to accompany him. If he succeeds, and I firmly believe he will succeed, it will certainty be' a great accomplishment for Canada, in view of the fact that so many nations have failed in their attempts. As to the intrinsic value of such an expedition to Canada, it is impossible for us to speak. There may be properties in that northern country which it may prove highly desire-able to take possession of in the name of Canada or of Great Britain. It is impossible to tell what minerals may be discovered, although Captain Bernier is not going for that purpose. But, taking it all in all, I
believe that aid given to Captain Bernier will prove a good investment for Canada, particularly if he succeeds. I have paid great attention to the two lectures which he delivered here ; I have observed closely his plan, and I believe it is a feasible one.
I do not believe there is any great danger or great difficulty surrounding it. I believe there are no difficulties that a man of the perseverance, determination and accomplishments of Captain Bernier will not overtake.
I believe he will succeed, and it will be a proud day for Canada if he does succeed.
I sincerely trust the government will entertain most favourably his demand.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much interest to the presentation of this case to the House by the several speakers who have addressed it, and I have no doubt that the encomiums that have been bestowed upon Captain Bernier are well deserved. But it does not necessarily follow, because we recognize his courage, daring, skill and general fitness for an enterprise of this kind, that we should give encouragement to an enterprise fraught with so much danger and having so little practical utility in view. When we look at the history of polar enterprise in the past we must concede that it has been one long sad story of disaster, suffering and loss. Nothing so far has been attained. The loss of Franklin and his crew, the voyage of Captain McClintock in search of Franklin, the expeditions of Scoresby, Kane, Greely and others down to Nansen and the ill-fated Andree, fill out a long story of disaster and intense suffering. What is gained by it all ? AVliat is proposed to be gained for Canada by this enterprise ? Nothing more than empty fame ; and I hold that at this period of our country's history this is not something that we should strive very hard to attain to. We have much more practical things to give our attention to. It has been urged that it might add largely to the territory of Canada; but I hold that additional territory is not one of the pressing wants of Canada. We have now more territory than we know anything about. We have large regions practically unexplored and as yet untrodden by the white man. If our attention is given to utilizing what we have without aiming beyond that it will result in greater benefit to the people of Canada. There are immense fields of enterprise opening up in this country in all directions-enterprises that are full of promise and practical utility for this new country, and that offer rewards far more certain than polar expeditions.
What advantage would accrue to this country, even supposing the North Pole were discovered ? Would it bring us more immigration ? Would it attract more capital ? Would it open up new avenues for trade and commerce ? Is there anything practical to be got out of it-anything ex-

396S
cept empty fame ? I am not denying that some practical results from a scientific point of view might be attained, but we have not reached that period of our history when we can afford so much attention to questions of this nature. There are many other practical questions with which we have to deal. It is said that the discovery of the North Pole would be a great advertisement for this country. Well, we unfortunately have too much advertisement of that character-too much advertisement of Canada as Our Lady of The Snows. What we require to do is rather to dispel the ignorance which exjsts regarding Canada's present territory and her climate, resources and productions. In doing this, we would be doing something which would produce practical results. I need not mention the hundreds of openings there are for practical enterprise in this country -openings in all directions, Everywhere appeals are made for government assistance to legitimate enterprises. I quite admit that to men who have a surplus of wealth, the project of Captain Bernier is an interesting one, and by all means let them expend some of their surplus wealth upon it. In older countries, such as Great Britain and other European countries, which have exhausted at home all the new avenues for enterprise, this scheme may be a legitimate one on which to spend government moneys. But in Canada I think there are far more practical objects demanding our attention and lying right within our reach. Appeals are made to this government again and again for assistance, which the government does not feel warranted in granting, extensive as are our resources. I did not intend to say but a few words on this subject, and I would only add that we should not forget that in contributing out of the national exchequer to a scheme of this kind, we are voting the money of. the poor as well as the rich, the money of the toiler as well as the money of the man of affluence. I do not see how we can well defend an expenditure of this kind, which can only result, at the best, in our acquiring a little empty fame, and which is far more likely to have the same fate that other similar enterprises have suffered, and furnish another sad story of a nation's folly.
Mr. IiODOLFIIE LEMIEUX (Gaspe). (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I fully concur in the remarks fallen from the lips of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) this afternoon. For many years back, Captain Bernier has shown that he has the skill, the technical knowledge, the pluck and the perseverance which tit him for such an arduous enterprise as that of the search for the North Pole ; and to my mind, that should induce the government to receive favourably his demand. The hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House (Mr. Richardson) told us that this enterprise had very little practical utility in view, and that he failed

to see what advantage would accrue to the country, even supposing the North Pole was discovered by Captain Bernier. Let the hon. gentleman allow me to tell him that but a few years ago the men who ventured to approve of the exploring expedition sent by the government to the Yukon were looked upon as visionaries. And who would now maintain that the country has not greatly benefited by those explorations of the Y'u-kon '!
It is said that if the enterprise undertaken by Captain Bernier were brought to a successful issue, it would be a great advertisement for this country, and that if a son of Canada were to plant the flag of his country at the North Pole, it would be a proud day for Canada. But aside altogether from the reputation that would accrue to Canada from this polar expedition, it must not be forgotten that this enterprise has a scientific object in view, which will be appreciated by all scientists and navigators. Moreover, the discovery of the North Pole in our case would not be a fruitless one. as it would enable us to establish our right to the unknown territories of the Arctic regions.
Captain Bernier was heard before several learned societies, the members of which are by no means visionaries, as my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) would have it, but practical men. Captain Bernier delivered addresses before the Royal Society of Canada, the Colonial Institute in London, the Geographical Society of Quebec and several other learned bodies, both in the United States and in Great Britain. The captain's theory has received the endorsation of all those learned societies, after they had fully considered its merits.
It often happens that the government encourages the projects of foreign scientists. Not long ago Signor Marconi's system of wireless telegraphy was adopted* by the government, and we shall soon be called upon to vote for that purpose a sum of $70,000. Is there a gentleman here who would venture to predict that Captain Bernier's expedition will be a barren thing for Canada, and that no tangible advantages will accrue to the country from it ?
On these several grounds, Sir, I think it my duty as a Canadian and as a representative from the province of Quebec, to endorse the demand made by Captain Bernier, and to express the hope that it will receive the favourable consideration of the government.

speechtext:
ROSS (Victoria, N.-S.) Canada has acquired some fame by sending her men to South Africa. She can add to that fame by assisting Captain Bernier's expedition to the north pole. Great Britain has spent a great deal of treasure and a great deal of blood in acquiring territory, and if we wish to be conspicuous in history, we must follow her example. I suppose that, even when we do discover the north pole, the market gardeners about Montreal will

hardly go there to grow fruit for sale. But, if you consider everything, I think it will be manifest that the discovery of the pole will be a valuable asset for the Dominion of Canada. It will elevate the history of the country and give us prominence in every country in the world. Our children's children will look back with admiration upon the history of the brave man who discovered the north pole and added this territory >to the Dominion. Captain Bernier has my entire sympathy in the enterprise he is undertaking, and I hope that the government will treat him in a generous broadminded manner.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: The speakers who have preceded me, and have favoured this request, seem to assume that Captain Bernier is going to be successful in his search for the pole, I think. I have read nearly all the records of polar exploration, and I am not satisfied in my own mind that Captain Bernier-and I will admit all that has been said concerning his bravery and ability-will come nearer to a solution of the problem than those who have preceded him have done. The argument put forth that it will be an excellent ad. vertisement for Canada, is, to my mind, an exceedingly specious one. It is an advertisement that will cost the country altogether too much, 'in my opinion. [DOT] I fail to see any good that will be accomplished by another polar expedition. And I do not think the people of this country would justify the government in the expenditure of anything like $50,000, or more for an expedition of that nature. We are told often in this House, and especially by hon. gentlemen on the other side, that the government is spending money too freely. The idea prevails, however, apparently, that the government has money to burn. It seems to me if they are disposed to use a free hand in the disposition of the revenues of the country, we can find a great deal more worthy objects and objects that will do a great deal more permanent good to the country than the discovery of the north pole. There are various ways >in which the money could be utilized either for colonization purposes or otherwise. But I think that Canada is too new a country and has too limited resources to justify the government in contributing any sum towards this expedition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
I have no desire to detain the House by repeating the many arguments that have been advanced by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) in support of the expedition of Captain Bernier tin search of the north pole. The hon. gentleman has placed the question so fully and completely before the House that nothing be need said along that line. Captain Bernier's energy and the zeal he has displayed in this matter, not only in Canada, but also in his visits to the old country during the past 125
two or three years, to say nothing of the many years previous when the people of Canada were not taking notice of him, must have commended him to every time Canadian. To my mind, if the north pole is to be discovered-and) I am one of those who believe that it will be dicovered-Captain Bernier is the kind of man who will discover it. I have given very considerable attention to the plans along whose lines Captain Bernier proposes to move in this expedition, and I think those plans will commend themselves to every man who informs himself upon the subject. Briefly, Captain Bernier is going to follow natural law. He is not going in opposition to nature, as be himself explains. Many of the explorers in the past who have attempted to find the north pole have failed because they went towards it from the wrong direction. But Captain Bernier, takes advantage of the discoveries with regard to the currents and the movements of the ice floes and of all the experience and the observations of others who have sailed in these northern seas, and L think he has a plan by which he will discover the pole, if it is ever going to be discovered. Now, some may think that the north pole will never be found. I understand that one man came within 230 miles of the pole, and another within 219 miles of it. If one navigator can come within 219 miles of the pole, why cannot another reach the pole itself V One thing is as reasonable as the other. Captain Bernier is of the opinion that Dr. Nansen went too far before putting his boat in the ice. The result was that he passed within 230 miles of the pole. Had he entered the ice 230 miles nearer, he might have floated over the pole and to-day have had the glory of being the man who discovered the north pole. Now, are .there any advantages to be gained by this expedition ? I hold that, even if it is an absolute failure there will be great advantages accruing to Canada from it. As an immigration advertisement nothing in the iworld that we can do with the same amount of .money would 'bring Canada so prominently and favourably before the world as this expedition of Captain Bernier to the pole. It, will be commented on by every newspaper throughout the world, and attention will be called to Canada on eveiy side. This will be a better way of spending money than some of the plans adopted by the Minister of the Interior at the present time. If there are any hon. gentlemen in the House who think we ought not to spend any sum for the purpose of assisting Captain Bernier I would suggest to them that, instead of spending $400,000 on immigration, by spending $300,000 on immigration and $100,000 to aid Captain Bernier, we should bring more immigrants to the country than if we spent $400,000 on our ordinary immigration service. What will the thing cost? If we do give Captain Bernier's expedition $100,000-and I am not aware that lie asks even that much-that sum will simply



amount to two cents per head of the population of this country. Where is the man, woman or child who would grudge that money in order that a Canadian may have the glory of being first to place the British flag at the pole. I am sure there is not one. We would all be proud as Canadians if one of our fellow countrymen could accomplish this great feat. In any case, we are not sending this money out of the country, I understand that the expedition will be fitted out here and every dollar spent in Canada. So, we are not losing the money, but are simply transferring it from one hand to another. We hear a great deal about the Alaskan boundary and tile trouble we have in settling the disputes between ourselves and the United States. Suppose that Captain Bernier fails to get sufficient assistance to enable him to undertake this expedition. If he goes to Washington-he is too patriotic to do so, but he would be justified, if he were turned down by this government, in seeking to secure assistance from some other country-if he goes to Washington, there is not the slightest doubt that, within twenty-four hours he will have all the money he wants. And the next thing we know we shall have another Alaska boundary question away near the north pole, with commissions sitting at Washington to settle question of our northern boundary. Is it not better to spend $100,000 and settle that question for ever ? The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) recommends various things that we might undertake instead of spending the money on this expedition. But I want to tell the hon. gentleman that there ds only one pole, and if we lose the opportunity now of sending Captain Bernier we may lose the opportunity for ever.
My own impression is that if Captain Bernier reaches the pole-there is only one North Pole, for we care nothing about the south, we have no possessions there-if Captain Bernier succeeds in reaching that pole and has the pleasure of wiring to us over the Marconi system the particular day on which he, ha's discovered the pole, I doubt very much if there will be another expedition going out there for years to come, because the ambition of every one is to be the first to find the pole. Now, I make this statement to show the government where 1 stand. I am not ashamed to say that I am prepared to stand by the government in any reasonable expenditure which they may make in assisting Captain Bernier. I know perfectly well that my constituents will support me. I do not believe in parish politics, I believe in taking a wide view of all these matters; and lam convinced that those who live after us will remember with pride that the parliament of Canada assisted Captan Bernier in being the first man to place the British flag upon the North Pole.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
McCREARY (Selkirk.) I am sometimes surprised at the consistency or Mr. HENDERSON.
inconsistency of some hon. gentlemen opposite. They complain a great deal of the expenditure this government makes year after year, and decry the large increase in the expenditure, and yet here they come now asking us to spend $80,000 ' or $100,000 on an object purely visionary or sensational. I think some of the older countries, such as Russia, France, Sweden, England and the United States, might possibly be justified in going into a little experiment of this sort; but for a new country like Canada to spend $100,000 of the people's money on such a visionary project as the discovery of the North Pole would be abject foolishness. I have no doubt that the hon. gentlemen who have just spoken on the other side would be glad if they could get the leader of the government to commit himself to such a project so that they could ridicule him afterwards on every platform in the country. That is exactly what they want, and I know it. A few years ago this country discovered what is known as Manitoba and the North-west Territories. That country they are trying to develop, that country they are not able to develop because they do not devote sufficient money to develop it properly. A few nights ago in this House grievous complaints were made by members from the territories that only a paltry sum of $357,000 was given them to govern 160,000 to 200,000 people. We have the same cry in Manitoba, the very same cry, that we cannot get sufficient money properly to run our government. Later on this country made another discovery, the Yukon territory. Now, I think we have done about enough discovery for some time to come. The North Pole will keep, it is in cold storage, and let it remain there awhile. I believe that if that pole was discovered it would prove to be one of the greatest curses to the premier of Canada. He would not know what to do with it, there is no doubt about it. There is a country around the North Pole, and the first thing we would see would be a big map of the country in the railway committee room here, with railways wanted by some great corporation. I have no doubt the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) would want a cinch on the water power to be developed, and some other hon. gentleman would want to run railways to Spitz-bergen and Greenland. I think the premier of Canada should take hard facts into consideration, and leave these chimerical schemes entirely for the future, until we become a big nation, until we have a surplus of funds on hand to undertake such a project. In the meantime, let us try to develop the countries that we have already discovered within the last 23 years, and which need more funds.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
If this scheme involved the expenditure of any considerable amount I would certainly hesitate * before asking the government to undertake

it. But we are told that all Captain Bernier expects from this government is $60,000, or one cent per head for every man, woman and child in this country. When we remember that some patent medicine companies expend three times that amount in one year to advertise their goods, I believe that if we looked on the expedition to the North Pole merely as an advertising scheme the money would be very well invested indeed. But, Mr. Speaker, there is a broader question than the mere question of advertising this country. Canada has contributed her share in the past towards making the history of this continent; Canada, I hope, has not arrived at that position where, for a paltry sum like the one now involved, she will stop in her course of progress, of discovery, of scientific research, deterred hy so small an amount as the one in question. We have had to-night testimony in favour of Captain Bernier from disinterested members on both sides of the House, from all parts of the Dominion. As a member from the province of Quebec, I am pleased and grateful for the tribute which has been paid to the valour and devotion of Captain Bernier. I believe Captain Bernier will reach the North Pole if that pole can be reached by the means which we have now at our disposal. He is a self-made man. At 17 years of age he commanded a ship sailing from ocean to ocean. He has since given his country a record of which he and his people have reason to be proud. His project has been submitted to and approved by learned societies, not only in Canada, but in Great Britain. The Society for the Advancement of Science, the Geographical Society, the Colonial Institute, and other learned bodies in Canada have approved of his idea. The list of subscriptions which has been shown us is headed by Lord Strathcona, one of the greatest of all our great Canadians, by Lord Minto, and by almost every distinguished man in this country. I believe that the government should give this matter full consideration, and not turn Captain Bernier away from this House as, in years past, discoverers of his stamp and value have been turned away in other countries. The course of Captain Bernier during the last two or three years, running from Ottawa to London, Horn Toronto to Quebec, from Montreal to other cities of the Dominion, reminds me of the efforts of Christopher Columbus some 400 years ago when he was asking Spain and the countries of southern Europe for assistance to enable him to discover a new world. Men were found by hundreds who failed to realize the value of his undertaking, but Providence inspired a woman, who will remain famous for all time, with the idea of contributing towards the discovery of tins new world. What the intrinsic value of this discovery may be none of us are at present able to say; but there is not a Canadian who would not 125J
be proud to tell his children in years to come that Canada contributed its quota to one of the greatest scientific discoveries in the world's history.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
I assume that I am a fairly practical man. I do not want to throw away my own money or the money of the country. But I think a country is not worth being called a country, a nation is not worth being called a nation, that is not able and willing to expend a little of its money in adventures. This is an adventure that, if successful, will bring, perhaps, not much practical result for the country, but will biing it a good deal of glory. The hon. member from Winnipeg (Mr. McCreary) thinks that Canada has done enough in discovering Manitoba, the North-west Territories and the Yukon .
It has been a great discovery and so far has been fairly costly. It will, I think, and I know in the future be enormously profitable, but it lacks one thing that is necessary in a man's life or a nation's life. It lacks any possible idea of romance, it is purely and simply practical-beef, wheat, pork and other things. I believe that if the small amount of money that is asked to help Captain Bernier in this expedition, it will not be an extravagance for Canada. I believe the amount can be saved ten times over to the people of the country by the reduction of many items in the estimates which we have had before us this session and which represent money that will be expended without profit or glory to the country. I believe that if this money is granted to Captain Bernier, it will, at all events, show the world that we Canadians are not altogether so wedded to what is only the practical -side, but that we have with us a little of that old romance that caused our forefathers to go to all parts of the world on voyages of discovery, and, as a rule not of profit to themselves. I think, we, in Canada, as the most northerly nation and the nearest to the North pole, might very properly grant the small sum that is asked to help on this expedition, which, if successful, will redound to the credit and glory of Canada and from a purely practical standpoint will be of no small advantage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) if he is in favour of the present government granting the bonus to Mr. Bernier for his expedition to the north pole ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: Certainly I am in favour of the persent government granting the bonus that is asked for.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would regret, I think, in future, if I allowed this opportunity to pass of speaking upon this great and important question. When Captain Bernier does discover the north pole, either with the assist-

ance of Canada, or with the assistance of some other government to which he will necessarily apply if Canada fails him, there will be many hon. gentlemen in this House who will regret that they had not some part in endeavouring to assist in this great project. I notice that two hon. gentlemen, the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McBwen) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) tried to introduce a political question into this matter, and one of these hon. gentlemen went so far beyond the record as to suggest that those of the opposition who are now advocating the expenditure of this money would be the first to decry the government in case they had acceded to the suggestion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: So you would.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) says : So we would. I particularly got upon my feet to speak, so that there will be no question about the position which I occupy upon this matter. I have, as a rule, the courage to say what I believe to be right and to act in accordance with what I believe to be right. Whether I may be right in this instance or not, is of course another matter. The people whom I have the honour to represent sent me here not necessarily to vote for one political party or the other but to exercise the best judgment I possess upon the various questions that come before this parliament. Some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House may laugh because I understand them to dissent from that proposition. Perhaps they do not understand an hon. gentleman acting upon that basis. I have confidence that if the people who sent me here to represent them should come to the conclusion that in the attitude X now take I have made an error of judgment, believing that I have done it sincerely, they will forgive me, but I do believe that this project will be successful. I believe that if there is a man in the world to-day who is likely to reach the north pole he is Captain Bernier. He is a native Canadian, he is a very intelligent and progressive man, a man who has faith in what he undertakes and it is a pity for Canada to fail to respond on this occasion to the opportunity which now presents itself of enunciating to the world the capabilities of the Canadian people. On the field of South Africa, the one characteristic that distinguished our noble citizen soldiers above all others, except their bravery, was that they were the people for an emergency, that they were capable people all round and that is the type of man who asks us to invest $100,000 in order to see if we cannot accomplish this great scientific discovery and incidentally advertise Canada in a way that nothing else could do. I want to say distinctly that the hon. member for South Huron and the hon. member for Selkirk, hardly appreciate the point when they talk about the opposition carping at Mr. LENNOX.
the expenditure of public money. There is a great and broad distinction between the opposition objecting to specific expenditures, because they are not judicious expenditures, and the suggestion of these hon. gentlemen. We are not saying on this side of the House that we cannot pay our way, we are not saying that Canada cannot pay for all she needs, that Canada is not in a position to pay money for anything that is in the interest of Canada, but the opposition do criticise, and it is the proper attitude of an opposition, expenditures of money in some instances because they think they are not wise or judicious expenditures. This is not a political question. It is a question for every man to exercise his honest judgment upon. It is a question for every hon. member to feel that whether it exactly suits his constituents or not he will, at this juncture, have done that which he believed to be right in saying that this small sum of money, comparatively, should in all reason be voted in support of this measure. I have little doubt that we will within a few years have the honour of having discovered the north pole.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
WADE (Annapolis.) Mr. Speaker, I do not purpose fnaking any speech on this occasion. I suppose that will be pleasant to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, but I wish to take my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) to task, because, when he saw the first suggestion of reformation upon the part of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, he should not have chided them with their past errors. They have complained, it is true, about the expenditures made by the government and we have not only stood by these expenditures, but we say that the government should go on and make increased expenditures. doing all things necessary for the welfare and benefit of Canada. I do believe that a small expenditure in connection with this matter would be an expenditure in that direction. We are not living in this world alone for the few dollars we may gather together ; there are other things which we have to live for as individuals. There are other things for us to live for as a nation : as a Dominion, and one of these other things may be possibly accomplished by the sending out of this expedition. It is not possible for any man to tell to-day what the result of it may be. Whether it will add to the material interest of Canada : whether it will demonstrate a great scientific problem or not ; but it is worthy an attempt. I regret that an hon. member on the other side of the House robbed me of one of the strongest arguments I had to make when he said, that it would only cost the country from one cent or two cents per head of the population. Now, there are some certain scientific questions which may or may not be settled by this expedition. We have all worried some of them. We have worried as to the reason why the needle points to the north ; we have worried

as to tlie variation of the compass, and why the compass varies more in one section of the globe than it does in another. These things may or may not be settled by this expedition, but I do believe that the country as a whole would support the government if they gave a reasonable grant in aid of this expedition which is being already aided by private enterprise in different parts of the empire. I simply wished to express my views in that direction, and to say that so far as I am concerned I shall be most glad to support the government in any reasonable expenditure for that purpose.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: If Captain Bernier does not get the bonus he desires for this expedition to the north pole, this debate will at least have done good, for I with others have obtained increased Information with regard to the project, and I must congratulate the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) on the able and eloquent manner in which he presented his proposition to the House. I am very sorry that at present I cannot bring myself up to the idea, that the discovery of the north pole will be of any use to us except from a sentimental point of view. It is not long since I read Nansen's ' Farthest North,' and the privations and trials that he endured are more than any person should be called upon to endure. If the country around the pole is anything like the country which Nansen traversed, we do not want such a country as that. That is my feeling, and I cannot get over it. I cannot help but think that the moneys which we would vote for this expedition could be much better spent in advancing the interests of Canada Internally. I quite appreciate the sentiment connected with the project ; the glory there would be in planting the British flag upon the north pole. I quite admit that it would be in that respect a grand and glorious thing. I may not be venturesome enough, but after reading Nansen's work I am apprehensive that no man can reach the pole. It is possible that he might, and if so I should be glad to rejoice with the rest r I should be more pleased to rejoice if the discoverer of the north pole were a Canadian, but at the present time I cannot see my way clear to support any appropriation for this purpose.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, personally I am certainly not insensible to the view which has been urged to-day upon the government by those who think that Canada should be the discoverer of the north pole, and that the efforts of Captain Bernier should receive some recognition. I largely share the enthusiasm of those who believe that it would not be a barren thing for Canada, if an enterprise which has combatted the efforts of so many brave and strong men were at last to be brought to a successful issue by a son of Canada. I do not share the views of my hon. friend from
Ontario (Mr. Ross). Even if there was nothing in that enterprise but sentiment, that alone is a thing which no nation can afford to be indifferent to.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
There is uot only the material prosperity of a nation to be considered ; there is also the moral elevation, the sentiment, the enthusiasm-all these go to make up a nation, and no nation can exist unless it proves itself to possess those qualities. But nobody can say that even from a material point of view there would not be something gained by the successful accomplishment of this project. From all accounts the north pole is a desolate part of the w-orld, but we have learned to believe in this age, that no part of the earth's surface however desolate is not productive of wealth. As was pointed out by my hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) we have lately found wealth where it was least expected-in the Yukon. I remember very well that some years ago the Yukon was ridiculed ; the very name excited scorn; but now we are glad that the Yukon is within our territory. We do not know but that perhaps there may be something in this enterprise if it were successful which would bring to us material profit. However that may be, and leaving aside altogether the idea of the material advantages, if a son of Canada were to plant the flag of his country at the north pole, if he were to achieve what so many brave men have struggled in vain to achieve, there is not a Canadian heart that would not beat with pride at the thought of it. Canada would be only too glad to purchase at a small cost such a glory. In Captain Bernier we have a man who I think is fit to take charge of such an enterprise. He has all the qualities which would lead us to believe that if that enterprise is to be brought to a successful issue, he is the man to do it. He is an experienced mariner ; he has enthusiasm, he has pluck, he has courage and he has the technical knowledge of his profession. If these qualities cannot discover the north pole it will not be discovered. At the same time I am not insensible either to the fact that Canada has many useful enterprises of immediate interest to prosecute, and between the two contentions perhaps it is difficult to come to a conclusion. The only thing that I can say is, that personally, and I believe, speaking also for some of my colleagues, I would rather be proud of contributing something to secure this glory for the Canadian people. I would have been more satisfied if my hon. friend (Mr. Charlton) who presented this ease with great force and great ability, had given us some idea of the amount which it was expected Canada should contribute. I never understood that it was contemplated that Canada should bear the whole cost of the expedition. I always understood that Captain Bernier had some enthusiastic friends who were ready

to help him, and I am told that he has now secured assistance to the amount of $20.-
000.	Well, I must confess my disappointment at that, for I had hoped he would have secured a much larger sum. He has received enconium, commendation and praise, but in the way of substantial assistance he has not received as much as one would have expected. Last year, in giving my personal views and after consulting with only some of my colleagues, I made bold to say that if Captain Bernier secured something of material assistance from private individuals in this country and outside of it. the government might perhaps come to his rescue and supply the balance. But I had no expectation that the sum of $100,000 would be asked from us. I see now that if Canada is to contribute anything at all it must be not less than $100,000. The views of the members of the House have been expressed generally, and if I understand aright, with very few exceptions, the members would be ready to sustain the government if they were to give $100,000 for this purpose. All I can say at present, and it is not to be expected I should say more, is. that the government cannot be indifferent to the views which have been presented here to-day. They shall receive due consideration, and if after having given the best consideration we can to this worthy scheme we come to the conclusion that it should be carried out, then, judging by what has been said here to-day, the government will be defended from the opposite side of the House against the charge of extravagance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that it was not purely in a spirit of ascertaining the material profit that we should deal with a question of this kind. There is a great deal of force in what has been said by some hon. gentlemen here to-day on both sides of the House, that in matters of this kind we have to look a little beyond considerations of that nature. I have had several interviews with Captain Bernier in regard to this expedition. While I have not been able to look into his plans as fully as some of the gentlemen who have spoken to-day, I am fully prepared to assent to what has been said with regard to Capt. Bernier's earnestness and capacity. He comes of a race who have been unsurpassed in past days in Canada in the spirit of adventure, in their efforts to discover and colonize the vast regions of Quebec, Ontario and the great West, as well as a considerable portion of the United States ; and Captain Bernier, I believe, has in himself all the qualifications which are necessary for making a success of that which has been attempted by so many individuals and by so many nations in the past. I do not overlook the fact that there is a great deal of this kind of work for us to do in Canada, or I mignt say in nearer portions of Canaua, if it be true, as hon. gentlemen have stated to-night, that Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the limits of Canada to-day embrace the North Pole. In the nearer portions of Canada there are a great many unexplored regions as to many of which we have not done our duty. But these are portions of the country which do not attract' the attention of the world to the same extent, and I do not think our efforts with regard to these would be handicapped by our giving a moderate measure of support to the enterprise of Captain Bernier. I would therefore say, so far as I am personally concerned-and in saying this I speak only for myself-that I would be inclined to give favourable consideration to a proposal by the government such as has been suggested by the hon. gentleman opposite.
