Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion of which I gave notice yesterday, I may in a few words state the case of our cattle trade as it stands to-day in Great Britain. We have heard a good deal about !t, but I do not think we have ever considered in this House the exact situation and the legislation of the British parliament as it now exists. Between 1878 and 1893, the British parliament adopted various laws, one after another, with a view to extirpating from the United Kingdom the different contagious diseases that were affecting cattle. Finally, in 1894, all these laws were combined in one statute, which is still in force, except ofie section, which I shall refer to later. This Act is called * an Act to Consolidate the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Acts, 1878 to 1893.' It is chapter 57 of 57 and 58 Victoria. By section 24 of that Act it is provided :
The provisions set forth in part I. (slaughter at port of landing) of the third schedule to this Act shall apply to all foreign animals other than'-
(a)	Foi'eign animals the landing of which is for the time being prohibited by order of the Board of Agriculture ;
(b)	Foreign animals the landing of which is allowed by order of the board without being subject under the provisions of this Act to slaughter or quarantine ; and
(c)	Foreign animals intended for exhibition < r other exceptional purposes, and the landing of which is allowed for the time being by ihe board subject to the provisions of part II (quarantine) of the third schedule to this Act.
Now, Section 2G of this Act gave to the Board of Agriculture a certain amount of discretion in regard to admittance of foreign animals at the ports of entry without requiring them to be slaughtered. In the third schedule of the Act, in the first part it is provided :
1.	The animals shall be landed only at a part of the port defined for that purpose by order of the Board of Agriculture, to be called a foreign animals wharf.
2.	The animals shall be landed in such manner, at such times and subject to such super-

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: As a rule the government does not receive with favour a motion made in amendment to the proposal to go into supply, but there are exceptional cases and this seems to be one of them. The subject which the hon. gentleman invites the House to consider is one of recognized importance, and the terms of his motion are such that I think they will find favour on both sides. Inasmuch as complaint has been made for several years, and a well founded complaint, that the regulations of the imperial government in relation to the cattle trade. are unreasonable and unfair as respects Canadian cattle, it is not out of place that we should express the opinion of the House with the view of bringing about a change if possible. The motion of my hon. friend is a respectful remonstrance against what we all feel to be an unfair condition of things. We do not question the right of the imperial government to make such regulations as may be deemed best in the interests of the mother country, and if these regulations were justified on the ground of what is called a protective policy, if it were declared that their sole purpose was to restrict, in the interests of English farmers, the importation of Canadian cattle, irrespective of disease, I do not think we would have any right to protest, because the question of policy is one entirely within the judgment of the imperial government and parliament. But when these restrictions are imposed because of disease said to exist among Canadian cattle, the government and parliament of Canada may well protest in moderate and respectful terms against any such baseless imputation. The government have from time to time made every reasonable effort to bring about a better condition of affairs. The Minister of Agriculture has done all that lay in his power to impress the British government with the necessity for a change, but has so far failed, and there is no reason why the Prime Minister, when he goes to London, should not bring this matter up in connection with others, and be in a position to show that he has the unanimous support of the House of Commons. Such unanimous support will strengthen his hands and perhaps enable him to convince the imperial government of the advisability of taking a different view from that to which they have so strongly adhered hitherto. We accept the motion in the spirit in which the hon. gentleman offers it, and hope it may be productive of much good.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: The motion which the hon. gentleman has just submitted is not at all in the language of that of which he gave notice yesterday, and I think it would have been far better for him to have taken a little more time and given the House an opportunity of considering his motion. The motion of which he gave notice yesterday was very different in its language from the one just submitted. It would have been far better, if the hon. gentleman proposed to modify it in the way he has done, to give notice of it and move it to-morrow, instead of giving us, at the conclusion of his speech, a motion which we really have had no time to properly consider, and which we cannot very well consider on the spur of the moment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will allow me-I do not think there is the slightest difference so far as the sense of the motion is concerned. But representation was made to me that toy leaving the word ' protest ' in the motion, it might be interpreted as indicating a desire on our part to interfere with the sphere of action of the British government and British parliament. And I .thought that was right, so I made the change. I think I made it still clearer by .basing the motion on the fact that we had given evidence to the British government that there was no more reason to apply the law, and .then I added tlie part about our foreign trade. As to the rest, the hon. gentleman will notice that it is exactly the same language, especially the conclusion as to the advantage the imperial 'conference will offer to the government in pressing the settlement of this question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
So far as the verbal phrasing is concerned, it is a great improvement on that which the hon. gentleman first suggested. For it would be impossible for us, I think, to pass the motion in the shape in which lie gave notice of it yesterday. It would be absolutely inappropriate and undignified for this parliament to pass such a resolution as the hon. gentleman told us yesterday he proposed. As to the present motion, I am not wholly satisfied with it, though I sympathize entirely with the object the hon. gentleman has in view. He says :
Evidence having been furnished to the British authorities proving that there is no justification for the application of the Diseases of Animals Act (Great Britain) to the cattle of Canada.
Are we not saying rather too much when we venture to suggest that ? Would it not be better to express our own opinions instead of commenting ou evidence furnished to the British authorities and declaring that that evidence proved so and so ? My only desire .in making this suggestion is to

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
have the motion pass in such form as will comport in every way with the dignity of this parliament, so that we may not suffer a rebuke for the wording of a resolution which, I trust, will pass the House without a dissenting voice. The mother country has a right to protect her home productions, either cattle or any other, in any way she sees fit. She has given us that right and she certainly can exercise it herself. The points we wish to make are two. In the first place we do not wish to have any imputation cast upon the condition of the cattle in Canada; and, in the next place, we do not wish our cattle to be excluded from the market of the mother country. I think that the Minister of Agriculture has stated in this House both last session and this session that, from his interviews and correspondence with the authorities in the mother country, he is fully satisfied that this measure is not continued for fear of any disease to come in from Canada, tout purely as a protective measure to the producers of the mother country. I have gathered that from the Minister of Agriculture's statements in the past. If I am wrong, I hope he will correct me. That toeing the case, it is not out of place that we should make representation to the mother country such as are covered toy the spirit, if not toy the words, of this resolution. I would like to point out to my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and also to the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) two considerations. Have they not given some grounds for the continuance of this embargo toy the change of the quarantine regulations which prevailed with regard to the entry of cattle from the United States into Canada ? Has or has not that point been made, in the negotiations, by the representatives of the mother country ? As I understand it, years ago, before this government came into power we had pretty strict regulations regarding the entry of American cattle into Canada. Since then we have admitted these cattle without subjecting them to stringent examination or quarantine, if we subject them to any at all. The result is that there-is more danger to the cattle of the mother country from free importation of cattle from Canada than there formerly was. That is one of the considerations which, I think, should be spoken to toy the Minister of Agriculture and as to which we should have some information from him. The other consideration is this-if it was known, as I suppose it was, in 1897 and in 189S that this was a purely protective measure to British industry, why was it that we did r.ot enter into negotiations for the remedying of this grievance at the time we gave the mother country the advantage first of 12$ per cent, afterwards of 25 per cent and still later of 33$ per cent in our markets ? Did not the Minister of Agriculture realize at the time that this was a protective measure to British producers V Did not the Minister of Finance realize this?
If they did not, what new light have they had on the subject since then ? And if they did realize it, why was1 some negotia-ions not had with the mother country in order to redress what my hon. friend from Labelle and the Minister of Finance consider a very serious grievance so far as this great Canadian industry is concerned 7 Would that not have been the proper time to consider the matter, instead of waiting for five years and then having a resolution passed which the right hon. gentleman will take home with him and bring to the attention of the British government ? If this is a protective measure, it would have been proper and by no means ungracious at the time when we were giving a considerable preference to the products of the mother country, to bring to the attention of the authorities there the fact that this was essentially a protective measure enforced against Canadian cattle entering the mother country and asking that the redress -sought by this resolution should be afforded. I think my hon. friend from Labelle was very enthusiastic in support of these measures brought dowu by the government giving a preference

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: Not very.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: At least, he was sufficiently enthusiastic to support them by his vote. Of course one cannot always perceive the future, but it might have been better if he had brought to the attention of his friends of the cabinet the considerations he has put forward so forcibly in his speech this evening. Now, I have not had time to scan the language of this resolution very carefully. I submit that it should not contain any statement of facts which it is not thoroughly in order for us to make. I am not satisfied that the wording of the first part of the resolution could not be improved. So far as the spirit of the resolution is concerned, and so far as the object with which it is presented to the House is concerned, I can only say that I am thoroughly in accord with it. If I can be satisfied that the language is in all respects proper and in accordance with the dignity of this parliament, I, for one, shall be inclined to give it my support.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
The government have done in this case What they could do in the case of any motion in amendment to motion for Committee of Supply, except one of direct censure-they have agreed to accept the motion as not being one of want of confidence. There have been many motions moved in this House in the past having for their object equally praiseworthy aims with this one which the government have called upon their friends to vote down because they were in amendment to a motion to go into Committee of Supply. The government availed themselves of that excuse, and their friends in justification of their position have declared that they did not want to vote
39S7

against the government and so voted against the motion. I am glad to know they have given us another example that it is possible to accept motions made on going into supply without regarding them as motions of want of confidence. This motion seeks to make such an impression on the imperial government that they will amend the statute as to admit Canadian cattle without the necessity of their being slaughtered on landing. We enjoyed that privilege before 1896, and we found it of considerable advantage to the farmers of Canada. For reasons best known to the imperial government they amended their regulations and passed an Act of parliament compelling the slaughter of Canadian cattle at the port of landing.
At that time this question was discussed at great length in this House. It was introduced for two or three years in succession by the present Postmaster General, then in opposition, and the government were taken severly to task as being responsible for bringing about this embargo on Canadian cattle. His contention was that the embargo was due to the fact that the regulations which we had made for transporting American cattle through Canada were laxly enforced, and the British people came to the conclusion that the disease could not be kept out from the United States, and therefore the embargo was put on. The Postmaster General, then representing North York, read a great deal of correspondence that took place between Sir Hector Langevin, a member of the Conservative government in Canada, and the home authorities, regarding this question, and he gave us a recital of the contract that was entered into between Canada and the mother country to ensure the freedom of Canada from importation of diseased cattle. In the first place the quarantine regulations provided that no animals could be imported unless they were detained at the frontier for ninety days so as to satisfy the people of this country that they were not in any way diseased. In the next place application was made to allow the Grand Trunk Railway and the Great Western Railway to carry American cattle through Canada on condition that they were accompanied by an agent on each train, that they should not be allowed off the train except at a quarantine station for the purpose of feeding, at which time the cars were to be run into an inclosure surrounded by a double board fence so there could be no possibility of the cattle in the neighbourhood coming in contact with them. After they were fed they were to be reloaded and passed through the country. All cars carrying cattle were to be disinfected before they were used for any other purpose. The cattle were to be inspected at the boundary line. It was afterwards found that the railway companies desired that the cattle should be inspected immediately upon landing. At first the cattle were inspected in daylight only, but after-Mr. SPROULE.
wards it was contended that the inspection could be made equally well at night if proper provision was made for lighting and so forth. The railway companies agreed to provide these facilities, and the inspection was made at night, and the business went on. Now, the whole contention of the hon. member for North York and of those who sup-jiorted him, was that these regulations were not enforced as strictly as they- should be on the part of the Canadian government. An endeavour was made to show how much Canada lost by it. It was stated that had the regulations been strictly carried out the embargo would never have been put on. The opposition concurred in those views, and the government were severely brought to task for negligence in carrying out those regulations.
Well, time went on, and there was a change of government. After the present government came into power they gave the country to understand that they would attempt to get this embargo removed. What was the first thing they did to that end ? It was to do away with the quarantine regulations providing that cattle coming from the United States should be detained for ninety days to show they were not diseased. That was one of the first requirements to convince the English people that there was no possibility of the disease being imported into Canada, and that requirement was abolished. Then the restrictions which surrounded the transportation of cattle through Canada were relaxed, and we have practically none to-day. Yet the Minister of Agriculture goes over to England and asks that this embargo be removed, after doing away with all the restrictions and precautions that were held to be so necessary by the English people to prevent the importation of disease from the United States, where it was known occasionally to exist. If the arguments that were then advanced against the government for not carrying out our agreement faithfully were of any weight then they have ten times more force against the present government. The present government have done the very thing that they should not have done, and they have left undone the very thing that they ought to have done to convince the British people that there was no danger in importing cattle from Canada into the British market. We were told in 1896 that the reason for this embargo being put on was laxity of enforcement of the regulations. But we find there was another reason.
I have here a report of a conference of the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture and Associated Societies held in Edinburgh, on October 9tli 1901. This conference took place with the Minister of Agriculture, and the desire of those associate societies was to get this embargo removed. In his reply he did'nt say the embargo was exactly due to the fact that he was afraid of the importation of the disease from Canada, be-

cause he admitted that it had been clearly demonstrated to the Minister of Agriculture as well as to the British parliament, that no pleuro-pneumonia had existed in Canada for a length of time ; and he said that was not the only cause of this Act being passed. But he said an effort to remove the Act would be unsuccessful for certain reasons. What were those reasons ? He explains what they were :
Then there is another idea abroad, that onlj Canada suffers, and that only Canadian cattle are effected by the present Act. But of course that is not the case. It applies to live animals all over the world, and in that respect Canada i3 exactly cn the same footing as any other country. Oh but, it is said, Canada is the only country where there is no disease, and therefore you should treat Canada specially. But ihat is not the case. The United States claim equally with Canada to be absolutely free from disease, and the fact is that we cannot differentiate between Canada and other countries. Once any other country shows, what is no doubt very difficult to prove, that it has a clean bill of health, you cannot stop at Canada. You would have to make an alteration in the law to affect every country that could supply us with store cattle.
And why can you not stop at Canada 1 He goes on to say why ?
One gentleman talked about undoing, not only the Act of 1896, but also any other arrangement made for putting all other nations on the same footing as Canada. You cannot do it. You cannot revise your treaties at a moment's notice ; and it is under treaties with other countries that we are obliged to afford to them exactly the same treatment as to Canada.
It is a wonder that our government never thought of that when they gave the magnificent concession to the British government of a preference on the importation of their goods. They were allowed a concession which was not granted to other countries. They were allowed a special consideration in our market and nothing was asked in return. Would it not have been an opportune time to have said to them : We give you a consideration which we give to no other country in the wjorldy We give you a special consideration in our market. Is it not proper for us to ask you to give us a consideration which you say cannot be done unless you give it to all other countries 1 Would It not be proper for us to ask you to cancel these treaties so as to enable you to give us a consideration which will be equal to the consideration which we give you 1 We know that the government made no effort in that direction. They were perfectly indifferent In regard to ft because there was not a word said about it. If the British government were right in their contention in 1896 that it was because of the laxity of quarantine regulations and because of the enforcement of other regulations which permitted the carrying of American cattle through Canada, and if this laxity was responsible for
the adoption of the embargo, I would remind the House that there are no regulations now at all. If the embargo was due to these causes before how can you expect, having removed these restrictions as to quarantine, without providing other regulations, to convince the English people that there is no danger of the possibility of the importation of disease ? We have succeeded in convincing them that there is no disease in the country. Then, we want to take a step further and convince them that under our quarantine and other regulations thire is no possibility of the importation of it. We have not been able to do that, anil the government have not addresed themselves to-that phase of the question. They seem to be perfectly indifferent to it. I think so long as our quarantine regulations remain as they are, it is almost useless to pass such a resolution as this, because the English people can answer at once by saying that there is nothing to prevent Uie importation of disease from the United States into Canada where they have had occasional outbreaks of pleuro-pneumonia in that country. They would say :	Asi long as your regulations remain as they are we shall consider it unwise to amend the law which prohibits your cattle from being imported into our country without being slaughtered at the port where they land. Last summer when the hon. Minister of Agriculture was home, when he incidentally mentioned that question and intimated the importance it would be to Canada to have the embargo removed, he did not make the effort he should have done to have it removed. He did not seem to go about it in a business way, in a way to convince the British people that there was no danger of the Importation of disease tv the admission of Canadian cattle, and that we thought we should have, some consideration for what we have done for them. It is all generosity on one side and all laxity on the other side, for while he boasted of giving a preference to the English people, he never took the slightest interest in asking them in consideration of that preference to do something in return, and give us a preference that they were not prepared to give to the United States or any other country in the world.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
In consequence of what the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has said in regard to this matter, 1 think it would be well for me to make one or two slight explanations. In the first place, I would say in regard to the wording of the motion, that while I did not see it until this evening, I take no exception to it in its general terms or to the statements of fact, which are there declared. The motion says that :
Evidence having been furnished to the British authorities proving that there is no justifica-

tion for the application of the Diseases of Animals Act (Great Britain), to the cattle of Canada, &c.
I have no hesitation in endorsing that statement. The evidence was so completely submitted to the Minister ot Agriculture iu England, [DOT] the Hon. Mr. Hanbury, that he first, privately, to myself, when I was interviewing him, acknowledged that there was no disease amongst our animals in [DOT]Canada against which the provisions of this Act ought to be enforced. When I suggested to bim that it would be well to make that statement publicly be shortly afterwards, in an interview, which the bon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) lias just been alluding to, made that state-i lent publicly, saying in answer to the assembly of the associations in Edinburgh that lie believed to-day that in Canada there was no contagious disease such as they feared the introduction of into England. We therefore say that the evidence has been supplied to Great Britain to show that there is no justification for the application of this Act as against Canadian cattle. Since I have spoken of the interview at Edinburgh, I would refer to the fact that the hon. member for East Grey has quoted Mr. Hanbnry's statement about the favoured-nation clause. He seems to think that this favoured-nation clause would interfere with any application of the Diseases of Animals Act. The two things have nothing whatever to do with each other. The favoured-nation clause applies simply to customs duties and has no reference whatever and does not in any way interfere with the application of Animals Diseases Act or of its relaxation. That was brought to Mr. Hanbury's attention shortly afterwards by myself through Lord Strathcona and an officer of his department wrote acknowledging that Mr. Hanbury bad made a mistake in making that reference to the favoured-nation clause, because it had nothing to do with this matter at all. As far as this motion is concerned, I have already stated on more than one occasion that I believe the people of Canada are unanimous in regard to this matter. I believe that everybody in Canada who has given the slightest attention to this question of the embargo on our cattle is fully convinced, in the first place, that no disease exists in this country, and, in the second place, that it was not necessary for the protection of the herds in Great Britain. I feel that the parliament and government of Canada can approach the imperial authorities on this question with the greatest force and strength. The line which is proposed by this resolution is exactly the line I took myself last year in Great Britain. It is following up with greater force the line which 1 took then, having a formal resolution of the Canadian parliament at its back, and witlT greater force because the representations would be made, not by the
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Minister of Agriculture of Canada, but by the Prime Minister of Canada, acting in his capacity as the plenipotentiary of this country at the imperial conference. I think it is well tnis resolution should be passed, that this enforcement and strength should be given to the Prime Minister of this country when be goes as the plenipotentiary of Canada to the imperial conference in London, and when he will be able to take the position wihich is here taken. There are one or two other matters which I would like to allude to. I feel no hesitation in asking this of the British authorities, because I am satisfied that in asking It we are not asking anything which will, in the slightest degree, hurt Great Britain. I do not wish to ask a favour from the mother country which she might think would hurt her people, but in this case we are asking something which will not only not hurt her, but which will really help her. It is a well known tact that the cattle-raisers of Great Britain do not wish to have Canadian Stockers freely imported into the interior of the country, but it is also a well known fact that a very large number of farmers in Great Britain who are feeders of cattle and who buy Stockers for the purpose of feeding them are very anxious that there should He Canadian stockers available for purchase. We also know that butchers in the large centres of Great Britain would be glad to have either our stockers or fat cattle permitted to be imported into the interior of the country, there to he slaughtered whenever it was thought best for them to be slaughtered.
They appreciate the fact that these animals, when they land at the six ports in Great Britain which are open to them, have to be slaughtered within eight days after their arrival whatever their condition may he. It not unfrequently happens that Canadian cattle, as well as American and Argentine cattle arrive in Great Britain, and are taken to the lairages after a tempestuous voyage, sometimes severely injured, it would of course be a great deal better in the interest of the food of the people, if these animals could be fumed out on pasture and fed for a while before being slaughtered. The butchers of Manchester, Birmingham, Wolverhampton and the inland cities where there are no lairages are all very7 keen to have Canadian cattle permitted to enter the country free.
My hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) has alluded to the quarantine between Canada and the United States. I have here the representations that were made last spring to the imperial authorities in a formal despatch from .the government of Canada to the government of Great Britain. It is distinctly stated in that dispatch that the quarantine of 90 days beween Canada and the United States had been removed iu 1897, and it is clearly outlined wby it was removed, and the well known fact is mentioned that in tbe United States for nearly ten

years, there never has been a single case of pleuro-pneumonia. It is stated that in consequence of the fact that in the United States this disease is unknown, and that the American people were fully convinced that this disease was not in existence and never had been in existence in Canada, the authorities of the two countries felt themselves justified in removing that 90 days quarantine. I have also here the answer of the imperial government to that memorandum, and in that answer there is not the slightest reference made to the removal of the quarantine between Canada and the United States. That fact is not given as an excuse in any shape or way for refusing to remove the embargo against our cattle. It was not considered to be a thing which entered into the argument at all, and I venture to think that if it were one of the chief reasons why the imperial authorities declined to remove the embargo as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) contends, the imperial authorities would have put it forward as a reason in their reply to our memorandum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: I did not say that so much, as I showed that the contentions of the friends of the Minister of Agriculture in 1896 were absurd, because if when the quarantine regulations were restricted it was sufficient to induce the British government to put on the embargo ; it would be unlikely they would remove the embargo when there was no quarantine.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: I was not in the House in 1896, but I watched the discussion pretty closely, and the contention then was that animals had come across the frontier and had been exported from Canada to England, in which the disease was found. We contended that these animals were not afflidted with pleuropneumonia and I think that was pretty fairly proven at the time. Sir Charles Tupper very clearly argued that then, and he thought he had proved it pretty conclusively. But if there was any danger at that time from animals coming through here, since then pleuro-pneumonia has ceased to exist in the United States. I do not remember the year in which these animals were supposed to be diseased.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Yes. As a matter of fact in 1897, when the quarantine between Canada and the United States was removed, it was clearly shown to me by the Bureau of Animal Industries in Washington, that in the United States there had been no known ease of pleuropneumonia for four years before 1897. As a matter of fact there were a few isolated cases in the United States in 1892, but from that to the present day there has not been known to be a single case of pleuro-pneumonia in the United States or in fact on
the North American continent. I can say this of our neighbours in the United States ; that they have to-day a very complete organization in their Bureau of Animal Industries in Washington for the supervision and control of contagious diseases of animals, which they are working from Washington all over the Union. Under these circumstances I feel that there is not the slightest reason for the imperial authorities maintaining the embargo because of any danger of pleuro-pneumonia coming from Canada or the United States. But I wish to point out, that if the imperial authorities are willing to remove the embargo and make it a condition that we should put the quarantine against the United States, we are perfectly free to do so to-morrow. We are free to do just as we find most conducive to our own profit and advantage. We have removed the quarantine between us and the United States by Order in Council, and we are free to impose it again by Order in Council any day, just as the Americans are free to impose the 90 day quarantine against us any time toy an Order of their Department at Washington. If any difficulty might arise from that, we are perfectly free and they are perfectly free to take whatever course we believe to be in the best interest of our own peoole. Therefore the argument based on that falls to the ground. I would like to add that I am perfectly satisfied that the imperial authorities appreciate and understand that there i,s no cattle disease in Canada. The reason which Mr. Hanbury gave to me, and gave to the people of England who interviewed him for the continuance of the embargo is:	That he believed it better, in the interest of the trade, to have a fixed statute rather than to have a regulation which might be changed from time to time. It is an ingenious reason and it is put forward pretty plausibly. I confess that it does not appeal to me at all strongly, and I think that it does not appeal to a very large number of people in England. He has receded entirely from the position that he was maintaining that embargo as against disease in Canada. I may say to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, that I do not think that I said anything which wotdd indicate that Mr. Hanbury or any one over there acknowledge that they were doing this because of protection to their cattle industry, or from a protective point of view, as we understand protection in Canada. Neither Mr. Hanbury nor Mr. Chamberlain nor any one I came into contact with, would acknowledge that. Whatever may have been their thoughts or whatever might have been the conclusion we might draw from their action, they have never acknowledged that they were doing this for the purpose for what we call protection in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: What I said was that the Minister of Agriculture himself had stated that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: I do not think I ever stated that. I am certain that I have never stated that, but I have stated this : That I was led to believe myself from their action that they had some such reason for doing it. But i never said that Mr. Hanbury or Mr. Chamberlain acknowledged it, because when I rather taxed them with it they distinctly disclaimed it and refused to acknowledge for a moment that they did this out of a protective spirit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: All I said was : That the hon. gentleman himself had stated that he was satisfied that the real reason they retained the embargo was because of protection to the British producers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: I think I have stated that, but I understood the hon. gentleman to say that I said that they had acknowledged this in England.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: I am glad I misunderstood the hon. gentleman, because I would not wish that impression to get abroad.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
Mr. Gill says in his speech before Mr. Hanbury :
The real question is that it is a battle between free trade and protection.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: Oh yes, some of the people in England have said so, but no official and no one in any responsible position has acknowledged to rue, or acknowledged so far as I know, that that is the case. I think myself there is a possibility, on such an occasion as the imperial conference between Great Britain and the colonies, of general questions of '*'commerce and trade between the different parts of the empire being taken up ; and I think that is a fitting occasion on which to discuss this question-to approach it on a broad and imperial ground. I think therefore it is well that the Prime Minister should do that, and it is certainly better that he should do it endorsed and supported by a resolution of the House of Commons, which would show that the representatives of the people of Canada feel strongly on this matter, and are unanimous in their opinion in regard to it.
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
I would like to make a remark or two in connection with the Murray Harbour and some other railway matters in Prince Edward Island. Any remarks which I may make need not be considered as adverse criticism of the money vote, because that vote is necessary, and the complaint I am making is that there is not sufficient money expended on the Prince Edward Island Railway. This Murray Harbour branch was contemplated many years ago. When the Prince Edward Island Railway was built in 1872-3, this section of country lying south of Hillsborough was left without any railway accommodation. Since then the people have been clamouring for this accommodation, and it is only lately that their request has been granted. This railway runs through an extensive area of country lying south of Hillsboro, some 30 or 40 miles away from any railway communication. The country is an agricultural one, settled by people who are frugal, industrious and honest, and as they have been contributing to the building of railways all over Canada, it is only right that they should receive some consideration. And though this amount may appear large for the building of the railway and the completion of a bridge across the Hillsborough, It is not anything too great in the interests of the people. This branch of railway extends from Southport to Murray Harbour, having a bridge across the Hillsborough to which tlie people of Prince Edward Island are obliged to contribute. It will become an important feeder of the Prince Edward Island Railway and eventually assist in largely reducing the deficit on that line. There are also other branches contemplated, and I want to call attention to the branch line in West Prince, which was also part of the scheme of building feeders for the purpose of assisting to develop the main line.
I refer to the branch line at or near Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
l
O'Leary station, on the west shore of Prince Edward Island, a distance of some 12 or 15 miles from the main line. The people living in that section have neither harbours nor wharfs nor any facilities for shipping their produce, and are obliged to haul their stuff a distance of 15 miles or so over pretty bad roads. Last year I brought the matter up before the hon. minister, and he said he could not have a survey or an estimate made of the cost of building the line then but he hoped at a future day to be able to obtain these. I hope that this year he will see that a survey is made between O'Leary and the western shore of Prince Edward Island.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: Between O'Learv and Cape Wolfe.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
I am glad to see that the miniser understands the situation. The building of that branch will prove not only a feeder to the main line but be a great benefit to the farmers and fishermen on that section of the coast.
I want also to call attention to the fact that Cape Wolfe is only about 20 miles distance from the shores of New Brunswick at Richi-bucto in the county of Kent. From Richi-bucto to the Intercolonial Railway there is a line of railway known as the Kent Northern Railway, which Is controlled by Mr. Brown, at Richibucto. If this branch were built to the west coast, there is commercial enterprise enough in that section of the country to place on a small steamer to open up communication with Richibucto. which is distant 15 miles, and communicates directly with the Kent Northern Railway and the Intercolonial Railway. This would develop trade there and afford greater facilities to the people. The people in the western end of Prince Edward Island have to go all around to the eastern part before they can ship their produce. This railway would very much lessen the distance, and prove of great advantage to the people. I trust the minister will order a survey and an estimate to be made, and I hope that on some future occasion we will find a sum in . the estimates to build, this branch line, which is so necessary to the people.
We know that in these days of progress more rapid transportation facilities are required. and the people who have not got these are absolutely out of the race. In the western part of the island, from Summer-side to Tignish, in the summer season, for about eight months, we have two trains a day running in that section. During the winter season one train is taken off, and the people are obliged to put up with the accommodation afforded by that one train per day. Realizing the difficulties under which they labour, a large meeting of the electors of West Prince was held in the village of Tignish last November for the purpose of discussing the matter. It was largely attended by the leading men of the district,

including four or five members of the local legislature and the Hon. Senator Yeo and other gentlemen of standing. At this meeting the following resolution was passed. And, if it would strengthen my claim at all I would tell the hon. minister that these gentlemen are strong Liberals and have always been so. One of them, the mover, is a member of the firm of J. H. Myrick & Co., and one of the greatest patrons of the railway, and the seconder is Rev. L>. M. Macdonald, who has been for thirty years parish priest of Tignish and that part of the country. The resolution is as follows :
Whereas the train accommodation accorded to West Prince is altogether inadequite to the needs of country, and little if any improvement on that afforded at the opening of the road quarter of a century ago.
And whereas one single train per day for this large and prosperous section of country is in nowise calculated to engender traffic for the road itself, since traffic only follows proper facilities.
And whereas, much if not all the enormous expense of keeping the road free from blockades would certainly be saved by operating two trains in1 winter ;-
Therefore resolved, that this mass meeting of the electors of West Prince, do hereby urge upon the Minister of Railways, Hon. A. G. Blair, the necessity of running two trains in winter as well as summer over this best paying section of our railway ; and further resolved that the representatives in the Senate and House of Commons be requested to urge upon the Railway Department of Canada, until granted, these altogether necessary improvements.
This resolution was unanimously passed at this large aud representative meeting of the electors of all shades of politics in West Prince. The meeting also appointed a committee composed of Rev. A. E. Burk, Mr. McFayden and Capt. Reid, M.L.A., to wait upon the manager of the railway at Moncton and also to see the minister himself with regard to this accommodation. These gentlemen, at great personal expense and at a busy part of the season, did see the manager at Moncton, and I understand also that some of them saw the minister. We expected that as a result we would have last winter this second train per day. Nothing was done. However, the second train was placed on the route a little earlier this year than last year-the 14th of April, as against the 14th of May last year-tout the spring has been a month in advance of last year. The minister knows that we have the two trains for eight months in the year, and surely he will see that for the accommodation of the people west of Sum-merside-some of them sixty-eight miles from Summerside-the two trains a day should be kept on for the other four months of the year. I trust the hon. minister will give tlie matter his favourable consideration and that he will find himself in a position to say to me this evening that we are to have the two trains a day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: Another improvement that is needed on the Prince Edward Island Railway is a new station at Alberton. The minister referred to this yesterday, and said that some day in the future 'it would actually be required. The station buildings at Alberton, Charlottetown and Georgetown-he provides for h station at Georgetown tin the estimates which we discussed last night-are three of the old stations erected by the contractors when they built the railway nearly thirty years ago. They may have been considered first-class buildings at that time. They are not only old, but they [are antiquated, out of date. The building at Alberton especially is rapidly going out of repair. The hon. minister will remember there is a ' Y ' at the station. If he does not recollect it, the deputy minister and chief engineer, who built the railway and knows all about it, will be able to inform him. The train coming from east or west, is obliged to back up a quarter of a mile or so to take the main line, a matter which involves not merely delay, but also danger to the trainmen and passengers. I trust that when the hon. minister builds the new station, which 1 hope he will do soon, he will do away with this ' Y ' nuisance. 1 shall be very glad if the 'lion, miuister can give me an answer this evening with regard to these matters.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member (Mr. Hackett) that it is not because I have not had the importance of these subjects very urgently pressed upon me Ibnt attentions baa not been given them before this, and that parliament has not been asked to give us money wherewith to make the improvements. 1 refer now particularly to the improvements [at Alberton, Charlottetown and other points on the main line. I am fully aware of the need of a good deal being done, but we are making such a large outlay with respect to the Hillsborough branch railway that i have not felt that I should be quite justified in taking up these works to the extent we might do at we h)ad not so large an undertaking on our hands. I sympathize fully with the view the hon. gentleman presents, and, for my part, would be well disposed to go as far as it is possible to go in order to meet Ins views. 1 have been pressed by other representatives from the island in the same direction, but have been obliged to say to them what I am compelled to say to the horn gentleman to-night that, they must exercise some platience until a more favourable opportunity offers for taking those things up properly. As to the matter of the train, I think that possibly something might have been done last winter towards establishing a second train during the winter but for a variety of causes. It was Into in the seasoin when it was taken up, and then the question was somewhat complicated by the proposal to establish connection be-

[DOT] tween Cape Tormentine on the New Brunswick side at the end of the Cape Tormentine Railway and the Prince Edward Island road on the other. Efforts were being made in thiat direction, and, until we knew just how they would develop, I was advised by the officers of the line, the final conclusion to run these trains as proposed, perhaps, had better not be pushed. While it was late in ithe summer season it was very early in what is called the winter season. Then circumstances personal to myself arose which really prevented me for quite a time from giving any attention at all to the subject. And so the season went by. 1 am only desirous, and, even at some cost to the country I would be willing to give to the people on the island a reasonably good service. I think (they are entitled to it, and I sympathize very fully with their wishes in that direction. I do not think I can say more at this moment. I do not think it would further the object in any way for me to make a more definite statement. The hon. gentleman will have to be content with the expression of my desire to go as far as I possibly can, consistently with all tlhe considerations that affect the question, in meeting the wishes of the people with respect to these trains.
Mr. HACIvETT. With regard to the second train, I am satisfied to let the matter rest with the minister, land I presume he will do right by the people of that section of the country. I would like to ask what the intention is with regard to the branch line from O'Leary to the west shore ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext:
That subject, though it has not been brought prominently before me, has been debated a good deal in connection with the Kent Northern Railway. Those who are interested in the Kent Northern Railway have in the public press and various other ways been urging it as a desirable road at all events in the summer season and to some extent in the winter for persons who wish to reach the island from the west in a most expeditious way. It would make a quicker and in some sense a closer connection than they now get by either Point du Chene or Cape Tormentine. But it has not been really urged upon my attention as an urgent question. I would not like to encourage the hon. gentleman to expect that, while we have in hand this Hillsborough undertaking, we would be likely to take up the branch line that he spoke of to Cape Wolfe. I think that will have to remain pending for a time. No doubt it has much to recommend it; but at present I am not able to express a decided opinion upon it.

Persons who are conversant with the names of some of the larger craft on the upper lakes will notice that many of these American boats * go through the Canadian lock and there is no question as to the superiority of the Canadian lock as compared with the American lock. speechtext:
I think that the ridings or counties that are abutting on this system of navigation, commonly known as the Trent Valley canal, can hardly find fault with the government for the manner in which they are treating them. Commencing with the year 1800 and down to 1901 there have been very considerable expenditures in connection with the works, running from $400.000 in 1890 to $486,575 in 1897, and amounting to $284,503 in 1901. The work has therefore been pushed with much more vigour within these past five or six years than heretofore. In connection with this work I am sure that if the general public knew the importance of it more attention would be paid to it. Let me tell the committee and the hon. minister that at the town of Peterborough there is being erected now a very large industry that is entirely due to the presence of this system of navigation.
I refer to what is known as a factory for the manufacture of cereal foods in which

some Americans are investing an immense amount of money, and I was told yesterday that they intend to start in a few month's with a daily consumption of at least 20,000 bushels of grain, so that the extent of the business may be realized. It is intended at this factory to manufacture these so-called prepared foods not only for consumption in Canada but for export to the old country. I was assured by a gentleman in Peterborough the other day that it was likely, that, if the canal had been an accomplished fact to Lake Ontario, they would have secured a very large iron industry a little time ago. I must congratulate the ministry on the fact that they have pressed this work forward and that they have accomplished a considerable amount within the past few years, but while this has been going on there are some sections of the work which, I think, call for some explanation as to why they have not progressed faster. Let me call attention to the construction of the lock a little below the town of Peterborough which I am pleased to say I saw a few weeks ago and which is really a wonderful work. I see by reference to the report of the hon. minister the following statement in regard to this work.
Section No. 2, Peterborough-Lalcefleld division. The cbntract for this section was awarded to Messrs. Corry & Laverdure, on May 21, 1896, [DOT]and the time for completion was fixed by this contract on November 1, 1897.
Here we are in 1902 and while, of course, a large amount of work has been done, that contract is not finished. I would like to know when that lock will be completed and in running order. The completion of that lock means that from a distance above Penelon Falls there will be, for 20 miles at least, a stretch of clear water to the town of Peterborough, and yet it is impossible for that long stretch to be utilized until this lock is completed ; not only from there but all the way down to Hastings on the eastern end. Yet, in this report it would seem that the completion of that part of the work was called for on the 1st of November, 1897. and is still in an uncompleted state. Can the hon. minister inform us when the lock below Peterborough will be completed which is covered by the Corry & Laverdure contract ?

The possibilities of this canal open up a new field of thought. It was looked upon for many years as being of a local character, but it is now demonstrated that it may be used extensively for the transportation of grain. I may tell the House that I know

from conversation with the owners of a large elevator at Midland with a capacity of a million and a quarter bushels, that they might have built their elevator at Buffalo, but that one strong reason that prompted them to come to Midland was that when this canal was constructed it would be a competitor for the transportation of grain, and that it would hold the railway rates in check. speechtext: I understood they had a claim against the government which was left to arbitration, and that the arbitrators have made an award against the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE SEARCH FOR THE NORTH POLE.
speechtext: They had a claim in the neighbourhood of between $320,000 and $330,000 and while the deputy minister could not certify the amount which they claimed or for any amount which would be accepted by them as reasonably satisfactory, we adopted the expedient of having the matter adjusted by selecting reputable and competent engineers who would advise the chief engineer on the subject. It was not an arbitration in the ordinary sense, but it was an advisory board of three engineers who would go upon the work and examine it and state what in their judgment would be a fail- allowance to make in respect to the claim. We selected Mr. Hobson and Mr. Surtees, and they suggested Mr. Brophy of the Public Works Department. We thought it would be impossible to have made the choice of any three men who would inspire more confidence or be better qualified to pass upon the question. They went into the subject very faithfully ; some items they rejected, with respect to others they made recommendation to the chief engineer, and as a result the claim is practically settled on the basis of an allowance of $126,000. I need not say that result was very unsatisfactory to the claimants!
